textbook_title: Building Clocks and Watches with MicroPython

questions.question_text: What does decomposition mean in computational thinking?

options.A: Writing the steps of a solution in a fixed order that always finishes
options.B: Noticing what repeats between different parts of a problem
options.C: Breaking a large problem into smaller pieces that can each be solved on their own
options.D: Hiding messy details behind a simple name so they can be ignored

questions.explanation: Decomposition splits a big problem, such as "build a clock," into small pieces like keeping time, splitting time, formatting time, drawing time, and handling input. Each piece has one job and can be tested alone. Option A describes algorithmic thinking, option B describes pattern recognition, and option D describes abstraction.

questions.question_text: Which chip is the microcontroller at the heart of the Raspberry Pi Pico?

options.B: ESP32
options.C: ATmega328

questions.explanation: The RP2040 was designed by the Raspberry Pi Foundation and powers every Pico board. It has two Arm Cortex-M0+ cores, 264 KB of RAM, and a 3.3 V logic level. The ESP32 and ATmega328 are other microcontrollers found on different boards, and the DS3231 is a real-time clock chip you will add to projects later, not a microcontroller.

questions.question_text: Why is a clock's display classified as an actuator rather than a sensor?

options.A: It uses more power than any other part of the clock
options.B: It is connected to the Pico with more than one wire
options.C: It measures how bright the room is around the clock
options.D: It receives signals from the Pico and changes something in the real world

questions.explanation: An actuator turns an electrical signal from the microcontroller into a real-world effect, such as lit digits. A sensor does the opposite: it measures the world and sends information toward the microcontroller. A handy test is to ask whether information flows toward the Pico or away from it. A display only receives, so it is an actuator.

questions.question_text: Which statement best describes how a microcontroller differs from a laptop computer?

options.A: It runs a full desktop operating system but with less memory
options.B: It is a small computer on one chip that is sized to control a single device
options.C: It has more memory than a laptop but runs much more slowly
options.D: It needs separate chips for its processor, memory, and input/output pins

questions.explanation: A microcontroller puts a processor, memory, and input/output connections on a single chip, and it often runs no operating system at all. It has kilobytes to a few megabytes of memory, uses milliwatts of power, and costs a few dollars. Telling time takes very little computing, so this small size is exactly right for a clock.

questions.question_text: Why do watch and clock chips often use a crystal that vibrates at 32,768 Hz?

options.A: The number is 2 to the 15th power, so 15 divide-by-two steps give exactly one tick per second
options.B: It is the fastest frequency that a quartz crystal can physically vibrate
options.C: It matches the 3.3 V logic level used by the RP2040 chip
options.D: It is the default clock speed of the Raspberry Pi Pico processor

questions.explanation: Because 32,768 equals 2^15, a chain of 15 "divide by two" circuits turns the crystal's vibration into a signal of exactly 1 Hz, which is one tick per second. This makes the crystal ideal for timekeeping. The Pico itself uses a 12 MHz crystal that is multiplied internally to 125 MHz, and logic voltage has nothing to do with frequency.

questions.question_text: In the sense, think, act pattern used by every device in this book, which part performs the "think" step?

options.A: The push button that reports when it is pressed
options.B: The buzzer that beeps when the alarm time arrives
options.C: The microcontroller that runs your program and decides what to do
options.D: The crystal that supplies the steady beat for timekeeping

questions.explanation: In a physical computing system, sensors gather information, the microcontroller decides what to do by running your program, and actuators carry out the decision. The button is a sensor and the buzzer is an actuator. The crystal supplies the regular beat that timekeeping depends on, but it does not make decisions about what the clock should show or do.

questions.question_text: A low-cost crystal is accurate to 30 parts per million. About how many seconds could a clock driven by it gain or lose in one day?

options.A: About 0.26 seconds
options.B: About 2.6 seconds
options.C: About 26 seconds
options.D: About 259 seconds

questions.explanation: One day has 86,400 seconds, and 30 ppm means 30 errors in every million ticks. Multiply 86,400 by 30 and divide by 1,000,000 to get about 2.6 seconds, or roughly a minute per month. This drift is why later chapters add real-time clock chips and internet time sync. The other options are off by a factor of 10 or more.

questions.question_text: Using the seconds-to-clock algorithm, what time does 3,725 seconds since midnight represent?
questions.explanation: Divide 3,725 by 3,600 to get 1 hour with 125 seconds left over. Divide 125 by 60 to get 2 minutes with 5 seconds left over. The result is 1:02:05. Writing the algorithm as ordered steps and checking it by hand on a real number, as the chapter does with 45,296 seconds, catches mistakes before any code is typed.

questions.question_text: Which list names the four core skills of computational thinking?

options.A: Decomposition, debugging, abstraction, and iteration
options.B: Decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, and algorithmic thinking
options.C: Sensing, thinking, acting, and repeating
options.D: Planning, coding, testing, and deploying

questions.explanation: The four skills are decomposition (split the problem), pattern recognition (notice what repeats), abstraction (hide details that do not matter), and algorithmic thinking (write clear ordered steps). Option C describes the sense, think, act cycle of a physical computing device, and option D describes stages of a software project. Debugging and iteration are useful habits but are not among the four skills.

questions.question_text: A clock shows `3:05` when it should show `15:05`. Using the clock decomposition table, which piece is the most likely culprit, and why?

options.A: Keep time, because the Pico has lost track of the seconds since midnight
options.B: Draw time, because the segments for the digit 5 are not lighting up
options.C: Format time, because it may be converting to 12-hour style when 24-hour is wanted
options.D: Handle input, because a button press has changed the current minute

questions.explanation: The display drew exactly what it was told, so "draw time" is probably fine, and the minutes are correct, so timekeeping is probably fine too. The hour is the only wrong value, which points to the piece that chooses between 12-hour and 24-hour style. Decomposition lets you narrow a whole clock down to one small piece in just two questions.

questions.question_text: Which equation expresses Ohm's Law?

options.A: V = I + R
options.B: V = I × R
options.C: I = V × R
options.D: R = V × I

questions.explanation: Ohm's Law says the voltage across a part equals the current through it times its resistance. Rearranged, it gives I = V / R and R = V / I, so you can find whichever value is missing. In a 3.3 V circuit with a 330 Ω resistor, the current is 3.3 / 330 = 10 mA. The other options mix up the operations and would give wrong units.

questions.question_text: By common convention, which wire color is used for a ground connection?

options.A: Red
options.B: Yellow
options.C: Green
options.D: Black

questions.explanation: Black wires carry ground, red wires carry power (3.3 V or 5 V), and other colors such as yellow, green, and blue are used for signals like data or clock lines. There is no law requiring this, but nearly everyone follows it, so a circuit can be understood at a glance. The display cable harness in this book uses the same scheme.

questions.question_text: Why should a 5 V output never be wired directly into a Raspberry Pi Pico input pin?

options.A: The GPIO pins are not 5 V tolerant, so the signal can permanently damage the pin
options.B: A 5 V signal changes too slowly for the RP2040 chip to read it
options.C: The Pico can only use its pins as outputs and never as inputs
options.D: The Pico always reads a 5 V signal as a logical 0

questions.explanation: The Pico uses 3.3 V logic, and its GPIO pins can be damaged by a 5 V signal. Going from the Pico to a 5 V part usually works, but the reverse direction is dangerous. Use a voltage divider or a level shifter to bring a 5 V output down to a safe level. Always check a part's datasheet for its logic level before wiring it.

questions.question_text: A red LED drops about 2.0 V and should run at about 10 mA from a 3.3 V pin. Which standard resistor value is the best choice?
questions.explanation: The formula R = (3.3 − 2.0) / 0.010 gives 130 Ω, but resistors are sold only in standard values, and 130 Ω is not one of them. You choose the next standard value up, 150 Ω, which gives about 8.7 mA. A smaller resistor such as 100 Ω or 47 Ω lets more current flow than planned and risks the LED.

questions.question_text: A voltage divider uses R1 = 1 kΩ on the input side and R2 = 2 kΩ on the ground side. What is the output voltage when the input is 5 V?
questions.explanation: The divider formula is Vout = Vin × R2 / (R1 + R2). With the numbers given, that is 5 × 2000 / 3000 = 3.33 V, which is a safe level for a Pico pin. If you swapped the two resistors you would get 1.67 V instead. The output is always taken from the point between the two resistors.

questions.question_text: A resistor has the color bands red, violet, brown, gold. What is its value?

options.A: 2.7 kΩ

questions.explanation: Read the first two bands as digits: red is 2 and violet is 7, giving 27. The third band is the multiplier, and brown means ×10, so the value is 27 × 10 = 270 Ω. The gold band means the real value is within ±5% of that. Forgetting the multiplier would give 27 Ω, and a multiplier of ×100 would give 2.7 kΩ.

questions.question_text: Why does an LED connected directly across a power source usually burn out?

options.A: Its voltage stays nearly fixed as current rises, so nothing limits the current
options.B: It becomes a very high resistance that blocks the current
options.C: Its anode and cathode swap places when the power is turned on
options.D: It converts the supply voltage into a higher voltage by itself

questions.explanation: An LED has a roughly fixed forward voltage, so unlike a resistor its voltage does not rise with current. That means the current is not self-limiting, and far too much can flow. A series resistor uses Ohm's Law on the extra voltage the LED does not use and sets the current to a safe level, often 330 Ω is a safe choice on a 3.3 V pin.

questions.question_text: Two part legs are pushed into holes a10 and c10 in the same terminal strip of a breadboard. What is the result?

options.A: They are not connected because they sit in different holes
options.B: They are connected only if a jumper crosses the center gap
options.C: They are electrically connected because the holes in a strip are joined
options.D: They are connected only through the power rail at the board edge

questions.explanation: Each row of five holes in a terminal strip is connected underneath as one conductor, so two legs in the same strip are shorted together. This is why parts must be placed so each leg lands in a different strip. The center gap separates the two halves so chips can straddle it, and power rails run along the edges as separate long lines.

questions.question_text: Why is the switching regulator on the Pico better for battery power than a linear regulator?

options.A: It converts voltage efficiently and wastes little energy as heat
options.B: It burns off extra voltage as heat so the output stays smooth
options.C: It raises the 3.3 V logic level up to 5 V for the GPIO pins
options.D: It stores charge in a coin cell so the board never loses power

questions.explanation: A switching regulator rapidly turns current on and off to convert voltage with little waste. A linear regulator simply burns the extra voltage as heat, so dropping 5 V to 3.3 V at 100 mA wastes about 0.17 W. Efficiency matters on a battery, which is why the Pico can run well from one. The Pico's pins stay at 3.3 V logic, and coin cells are used only for real-time clocks.

questions.question_text: A display shows nothing. A multimeter set to DC voltage across the display's VCC and GND pins reads 3.3 V. What does this reading most strongly suggest?

options.A: Power never arrived at the display, so the power wire is broken
options.B: The ground wire is missing, so the display has no return path
options.C: The Pico is damaged, so the display cannot be powered
options.D: Power is arriving correctly, so the fault is elsewhere, such as a data wire

questions.explanation: A reading of 3.3 V between VCC and GND proves the display has both power and ground. A reading of 0 V would mean power never arrived, and a missing ground would also prevent a proper reading. With power confirmed, you continue the search at the next suspect, such as a loose or misplaced data wire. A multimeter turns guessing into a step-by-step diagnosis.

questions.chapter: MicroPython Basics: Variables and Data Types
questions.question_text: What does the REPL do with each line you type at the `>>>` prompt?

options.A: It saves the line to a file and runs the file when you press Stop
options.B: It compiles your whole program on the laptop and sends the result to the Pico
options.C: It reads the line, evaluates it, prints the result, and loops back for more
options.D: It waits for a complete program to be uploaded before running anything

questions.explanation: REPL stands for Read-Eval-Print Loop. It reads what you typed, evaluates it, prints the answer, and loops back for the next line. This gives you instant feedback, so you can test a command in five seconds before adding it to a program. Typing an expression like `2 + 3` shows its value automatically, while `print()` shows exactly what you give it.

questions.chapter: MicroPython Basics: Variables and Data Types
questions.question_text: What does the `//` operator do in MicroPython?

options.A: It divides and discards the remainder, giving a whole number
options.B: It divides and returns only the remainder
options.C: It divides and always returns a number with a decimal point
options.D: It raises the first number to the power of the second

questions.explanation: The `//` operator is floor division, so `7 // 2` is 3. The `%` operator returns only the remainder, so `7 % 2` is 1. The `/` operator always returns a float, so `7 / 2` is 3.5, and `**` raises to a power. Clock programs use `//` and `%` together to split a number of seconds into hours, minutes, and seconds.

questions.chapter: MicroPython Basics: Variables and Data Types
questions.question_text: Which collection type cannot be changed after it is created, and is what `localtime()` returns?

options.A: List
options.B: Dictionary
options.C: Float
options.D: Tuple

questions.explanation: A tuple is an ordered collection like a list, but it is immutable. The `localtime()` function returns the current time as an 8-item tuple of year, month, day, hour, minute, second, weekday, and year day. Colors are also tuples, such as `(255, 0, 0)` for red. Lists and dictionaries can change, and a float is a single number, not a collection.

questions.chapter: MicroPython Basics: Variables and Data Types
questions.question_text: Why can using `/` to compute a pixel position cause an error?

options.A: The `/` operator can only be used with negative numbers
options.B: The `/` operator always returns a float such as `3.0`, not a whole number
options.C: The `/` operator discards the remainder and returns zero
options.D: The `/` operator works only on strings, not on numbers

questions.explanation: Division with `/` always returns a float, even when the answer is whole, so `6 / 2` gives `3.0`. Code that needs a whole number, such as a pixel position or a list index, can break on that hidden float. Use `//` for whole-number division, or convert the result with `int()` or `round()`. Remember that `int(3.9)` drops the decimal part, while `round(3.9)` gives 4.

questions.chapter: MicroPython Basics: Variables and Data Types
questions.question_text: Thonny cannot find your Pico even though it is plugged in. What is the most common cause?

options.A: The Pico has run out of its 264 KB of RAM
options.B: The editor is saving files to the computer instead of the device
options.C: The program uses an f-string on an older firmware version
options.D: The USB cable only carries power and has no data wires

questions.explanation: Many cheap USB cables are charge-only and contain no data wires, so the Pico powers up but never appears as a serial port. Try a different cable, ideally one you know can transfer files, and plug it directly into the computer instead of a hub. The other options affect how a program behaves after the connection already works, not whether Thonny can find the board.

questions.chapter: MicroPython Basics: Variables and Data Types
questions.question_text: Why is MicroPython described as a subset of Python 3?

options.A: It includes the core language and a trimmed library, plus extra hardware modules like `machine`
options.B: It is an older version of Python that was written before Python 3
options.C: It must be compiled on a laptop before the code can run on the Pico
options.D: It supports only whole numbers and has no floating-point type

questions.explanation: The full Python interpreter would not fit on a chip with 264 KB of RAM, so MicroPython keeps the core language and a smaller standard library, then adds modules such as `machine`, `neopixel`, and `rp2` for hardware. If a program from the internet fails with `ImportError`, check whether that module exists in MicroPython. It does support floats, with about 7 significant digits.

questions.chapter: MicroPython Basics: Variables and Data Types
questions.question_text: What does the expression `(hour24 + 11) % 12 + 1` produce when `hour24` is 0?
questions.explanation: Add 11 to get 11, take the remainder when divided by 12 to get 11, then add 1 to get 12. The plain remainder `hour % 12` would give 0 for midnight, but a 12-hour clock should show 12. The same formula gives 12 for hour 12 and 1 for hour 13, so testing the edge cases confirms that it works for the whole day.

questions.chapter: MicroPython Basics: Variables and Data Types
questions.question_text: With `hour = 9` and `minute = 5`, what does `print(f"{hour:02d}:{minute:02d}")` display?
questions.explanation: The format specifier `02d` means an integer at least two characters wide, padded with zeros. Applying it to both values turns 9 into `09` and 5 into `05`. Without the specifier, the clock would show `9:5`, which looks broken. The older `.format()` method does the same job and works on every MicroPython version, while f-strings need reasonably recent firmware.

questions.chapter: MicroPython Basics: Variables and Data Types
questions.question_text: Given `total = 3725`, what value does `minutes` hold after `left = total % 3600` and `minutes = left // 60`?
questions.explanation: The expression `3725 % 3600` leaves 125 seconds after removing one whole hour. Then `125 // 60` gives 2 whole minutes, with 5 seconds remaining. So the time is 1 hour, 2 minutes, and 5 seconds. The value 62 would be the total number of minutes, which ignores the step of separating hours from the leftover seconds.

questions.chapter: MicroPython Basics: Variables and Data Types
questions.question_text: A program stops with a `TypeError` on the line `print("Hour: " + hour)`. Adding `print(type(hour))` shows `<class 'int'>`. What does this reveal and how should you fix it?

options.A: The variable name is a reserved word, so it must be renamed
options.B: Concatenation needs strings, so convert with `str(hour)` or use an f-string
options.C: The variable is a float, so it should be rounded with `round()`
options.D: The variable is a tuple, so it must be unpacked before printing

questions.explanation: The `+` operator joins strings only with strings, and `hour` is an integer. Print debugging with `type()` revealed the mismatch. You can fix it with `"Hour: " + str(hour)`, or more cleanly with an f-string such as `f"Hour: {hour}"`. Printing a value and its type is often the quickest way to uncover a hidden string, float, or integer.

questions.question_text: Which statement exits a loop immediately?

options.A: `continue`
options.B: `break`
options.C: `pass`
options.D: `global`

questions.explanation: The `break` statement leaves the loop at once, while `continue` skips only the rest of the current pass and moves to the next one. In the chapter's example, a loop over `range(10)` skips 3 with `continue` and stops at 6 with `break`, so it prints 0, 1, 2, 4, and 5. The `global` keyword has nothing to do with loop control.

questions.question_text: Which built-in MicroPython module provides the `Pin`, `I2C`, `SPI`, `PWM`, and `ADC` classes?

options.A: `time`
options.B: `framebuf`
options.C: `neopixel`
options.D: `machine`

questions.explanation: The `machine` module is MicroPython's gateway to the Pico's hardware, and you will import from it in almost every lab. The `time` module handles delays and clock values, `framebuf` draws to a memory buffer, and `neopixel` controls NeoPixel LEDs. The `machine` module also offers utilities such as `machine.freq()` and `machine.reset()`.

questions.question_text: How does a module differ from a library in MicroPython?

options.A: A module is a single `.py` file, and a library is a collection of related modules
options.B: A module is built into the Pico, and a library is always copied from a computer
options.C: A module holds only classes, and a library holds only variables
options.D: A module runs on core 0, and a library runs on core 1

questions.explanation: A module is one Python file whose name, without `.py`, becomes the name you import. A library groups modules that provide a set of related features. Some libraries are built in, such as `machine`, and others are added by copying files to the Pico, such as `ssd1306`. Modules can hold functions, variables, and classes, and neither is tied to a particular processor core.

questions.question_text: Starting with `seconds = 58`, what is its value after the line `seconds = (seconds + 1) % 60` runs four times?
questions.explanation: The four passes produce 59, 0, 1, and 2. The `% 60` operator wraps the value back to 0 once it would reach 60, just like the numbers on a clock face. Without the modulo, the counter would reach 62. This wrap-around trick works for seconds, minutes, hours, and menu modes, and it handles going backward too.

questions.question_text: With `hour = 8`, what does `greeting` become in this chain: `if hour < 6` Night, `elif hour < 12` Morning, `elif hour < 18` Afternoon, `else` Evening?

options.A: Night
options.B: Morning
options.C: Afternoon
options.D: Evening

questions.explanation: Python tests the conditions from the top and runs only the first block whose condition is true. Here `8 < 6` is false and `8 < 12` is true, so `greeting` is "Morning" and the remaining tests are skipped. Order matters: if the `hour < 18` test came first, every morning would also be called "Afternoon".

questions.question_text: Why does the line `if hour = 12:` cause a syntax error?

options.A: The number 12 is too large to use in a condition
options.B: The `if` statement must be written with parentheses around it
options.C: The `time` module must be imported before any `if` statement
options.D: A single `=` stores a value, so a comparison needs `==`

questions.explanation: In Python, `=` is the assignment operator that stores a value, and `==` asks whether two values are equal. A condition needs a comparison that produces a boolean, so `if hour == 12:` is correct. If an `if` line still fails, check the colon at the end and the indentation of the block underneath. Those are the other two usual suspects.

questions.question_text: Which loop prints the five-minute-style marks 0, 15, 30, and 45 and nothing else?

options.A: `for m in range(0, 60, 15):`
options.B: `for m in range(0, 45, 15):`
options.C: `for m in range(15, 60, 15):`
options.D: `for m in range(0, 15, 60):`

questions.explanation: The `range(start, stop, step)` function stops before the stop value, so `range(0, 60, 15)` yields 0, 15, 30, and 45. Option B stops at 30 because 45 is excluded, option C skips 0 and starts at 15, and option D yields only 0 because the step is larger than the gap. Counting how many values you need helps you check the stop value.

questions.question_text: Why would `count += 1` inside a function raise an error unless the function declares `global count`?

options.A: Functions are not allowed to change integer values
options.B: The word `count` is reserved by Python for loops
options.C: Assigning inside a function creates a new local variable that has no value yet
options.D: The `+=` operator works only on lists and strings

questions.explanation: Assigning to a name inside a function normally creates a new local variable. Since `count += 1` needs a starting value, and the local `count` does not have one, Python raises an error. The `global` keyword tells Python to use the variable defined outside the function. Use it sparingly, though interrupt handlers and callbacks often need it because they cannot return a value to your main code.

questions.question_text: You create `seconds = Counter(60)` and `minutes = Counter(60)`, then call `seconds.tick()` five times. What is `minutes.value`, and why?

options.A: 5, because both objects share one value stored in the class
options.B: 5, because `tick()` updates every object built from `Counter`
options.C: 60, because the limit is applied to every object at once
options.D: 0, because each object keeps its own copy of `value`

questions.explanation: A class is a blueprint, and each object built from it stores its own data. The `__init__` method sets `self.value = 0` separately for `seconds` and for `minutes`, and `tick()` changes only the object it is called on. That is why one program can run several counters without interference. Calling `seconds.tick()` leaves `minutes` untouched.

questions.question_text: Why is `except OSError:` usually better than a bare `except:` when reading a sensor that might be unplugged?

options.A: It handles only the failure you expect, so unrelated bugs are not hidden
options.B: It makes the program run faster than a bare `except:` block
options.C: It prevents the sensor from ever being unplugged during a run
options.D: It lets the program skip the `try` block entirely

questions.explanation: Talking to an unplugged device raises `OSError`, and naming that exception lets your code print a helpful message or use a fallback. A bare `except:` catches every exception, including typos and logic errors, which hides real bugs and makes them hard to find. Naming the exception you expect keeps the handler focused and keeps unexpected problems visible.

questions.chapter: The Pico Platform: Pins, Files, and Firmware
questions.question_text: A wire is connected to the pin labeled GP15, which is physical pin 20 on the board. Which number do you write inside `Pin()` in your code?
questions.explanation: Your code always uses the GP number, so you write `Pin(15)`. The physical pin number only describes where the pin sits on the board, counted from a corner. Typing the physical number into `Pin()` is a very common mistake that lights the wrong pin or none at all. Always look up the GP label on a pinout diagram.

questions.chapter: The Pico Platform: Pins, Files, and Firmware
questions.question_text: In what order does MicroPython run the two special files when the Pico powers on?

options.A: `main.py` first, then `boot.py`
options.B: `config.py` first, then `main.py`
options.C: `boot.py` first, then `main.py`
options.D: `main.py` first, then the `/lib` folder

questions.explanation: The file `boot.py` runs first and is for low-level setup, so it is usually left empty. The file `main.py` runs next and holds your clock program. To make a clock start by itself with no computer attached, save the program on the Pico as `main.py`. A program with any other name runs only when you press Run in Thonny.

questions.chapter: The Pico Platform: Pins, Files, and Firmware
questions.question_text: Why does a program saved on the Pico survive a power loss, while the variables it was using disappear?

options.A: Flash is faster than RAM, so it needs power to hold its data
options.B: Flash keeps its contents without power, while RAM is wiped when power is lost
options.C: RAM holds the firmware and your files, while flash holds the variables
options.D: Both are wiped at power-off, but flash restores itself from the USB cable

questions.explanation: The Pico has 2 MB of flash that holds the MicroPython firmware and your files, and it keeps them with no power. The 264 KB of RAM is fast working memory for variables, and it is wiped whenever power is lost. Think of flash as a bookshelf and RAM as a desk. Flash also wears out after about 100,000 erase cycles per block.

questions.chapter: The Pico Platform: Pins, Files, and Firmware
questions.question_text: What problem does a pull-up resistor solve for a button connected to an input pin?

options.A: It increases the current so the pin can drive an LED directly
options.B: It converts a 5 V button signal into a safe 3.3 V signal
options.C: It removes the contact bounce that happens when a button is pressed
options.D: It gives the pin a defined resting level so it does not float with noise

questions.explanation: An input connected to nothing floats, so its voltage drifts with static electricity and `value()` flips unpredictably between 0 and 1. A pull-up connects the pin to 3.3 V through a large resistor, so it reads 1 by default. Pressing the button connects the pin to ground, which reads 0. Debouncing is a separate problem that Chapter 7 covers.

questions.chapter: The Pico Platform: Pins, Files, and Firmware
questions.question_text: Why do the buttons in this book need only two connections, one to a GPIO pin and one to ground?

options.A: The RP2040 has an internal pull-up that you switch on with `Pin.PULL_UP`
options.B: Every button has a resistor built into its plastic case
options.C: GPIO pins are always connected to ground inside the chip
options.D: The wireless chip on the Pico W supplies the resting voltage

questions.explanation: Every GPIO pin has a built-in resistor of roughly 50 to 80 kΩ that you enable in code with `Pin.PULL_UP`. That saves parts and wiring because no external resistor is needed. The button then simply connects the pin to ground when pressed. This also works on the plain Pico, which has no wireless chip at all.

questions.chapter: The Pico Platform: Pins, Files, and Firmware
questions.question_text: A button is wired between GP10 and ground, and the pin is configured with `Pin.PULL_UP`. What does `value()` return while the button is pressed?

options.B: None

questions.explanation: With the pull-up, an unpressed button leaves the pin at 3.3 V, so `value()` is 1. Pressing the button connects the pin to ground and overpowers the weak pull-up, so `value()` is 0. This backward-feeling behavior is called active low, and it is the standard way to wire buttons. The method returns only 0 or 1, never a voltage.

questions.chapter: The Pico Platform: Pins, Files, and Firmware
questions.question_text: You downloaded a new `.uf2` MicroPython firmware file. What must you do to make the `RPI-RP2` drive appear so you can drag the file onto it?

options.A: Press Ctrl+D in the Shell panel of Thonny
options.B: Hold the BOOTSEL button while plugging the Pico into USB
options.C: Save a program on the Pico with the name `main.py`
options.D: Run `os.uname()` in the REPL and copy the version text

questions.explanation: Holding BOOTSEL while plugging in makes the Pico present itself as a USB drive named `RPI-RP2`. Drag the `.uf2` file onto that drive and the Pico reboots by itself with the new firmware. Thonny's Install MicroPython option can do this for you. Choose the firmware file for your exact board, since a plain Pico file will not give a Pico W any WiFi.

questions.chapter: The Pico Platform: Pins, Files, and Firmware
questions.question_text: Your clock kit uses `config.py` with a line `BUTTON_PIN = 14`. You move the button wire to GP16. What is the best change to make?

options.A: Edit every program that creates a button and replace 14 with 16
options.B: Reflash the firmware so the Pico learns about the new pin
options.C: Rename `main.py` so that the Pico rereads its pin settings
options.D: Change `BUTTON_PIN` to 16 once in `config.py`

questions.explanation: The config file pattern keeps every hardware setting in one file that other programs import. Changing a single line updates every program that uses `config.BUTTON_PIN`. Without this pattern, pin numbers are scattered through many files and rewiring means editing dozens of lines. Adding a comment naming the wire color next to each pin also turns the file into a wiring diagram.

questions.chapter: The Pico Platform: Pins, Files, and Firmware
questions.question_text: A clock program works when you press Run in Thonny, but nothing happens after you unplug and replug the Pico. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The file `boot.py` runs first and always erases the program
options.B: The flash memory has worn out after only a few runs
options.C: The program was not saved on the Pico as `main.py`
options.D: The Pico W firmware is missing from the board

questions.explanation: Only a file named `main.py` on the Pico runs automatically at power-on. A program with another name, or one saved only on the computer, runs only when you press Run. Check with `os.listdir()` that the file arrived. Flash wear takes about 100,000 erase cycles per block, so a few runs cannot cause it, and `boot.py` is normally empty.

questions.chapter: The Pico Platform: Pins, Files, and Firmware
questions.question_text: A program fails on the line `from machine import Pin` with a `ModuleNotFoundError`, even though the same code worked yesterday. What should you check first?

options.A: Whether Thonny's interpreter was switched to Local Python 3
options.B: Whether the `machine` file was copied into the `/lib` folder
options.C: Whether the Pico has run out of its 264 KB of RAM
options.D: Whether the firmware is too old to support f-strings

questions.explanation: The `machine` module exists only in MicroPython on the Pico. If Thonny's interpreter is set to Local Python 3, your code runs on the computer, where that module does not exist, and the import fails. Look at the bottom-right corner of the Thonny window and select MicroPython (Raspberry Pi Pico). The `machine` module is built in, so it never needs to be copied to `/lib`.

questions.question_text: In the time tuple returned by `localtime()`, which weekday number represents Monday?
questions.explanation: The weekday field runs from 0 to 6, where Monday is 0 and Sunday is 6. It is not Sunday-first as in some calendars. For example, September 28, 2026 is a Monday, so its weekday number is 0. Because the weekday already starts at 0, it can be used directly as an index into a list of day names.

questions.question_text: Which slice of `time.localtime()` returns the hour, minute, and second?
questions.explanation: The tuple fields are year (0), month (1), day (2), hour (3), minute (4), second (5), weekday (6), and yearday (7). A slice stops before its end index, so `[3:6]` returns positions 3, 4, and 5. The slice `[0:3]` returns the calendar date, `[3:5]` misses the seconds, and `[4:7]` starts at the minute. Writing `hour, minute, second = time.localtime()[3:6]` is the heart of nearly every clock program.

questions.question_text: A clock shows a date in 2021 after the Pico is powered from a wall adapter. Why?

options.A: The `localtime()` function always returns a Unix timestamp from 1970
options.B: Thonny erases the stored date whenever the Pico is disconnected
options.C: Plain MicroPython has no clock battery, so it forgets the time without power
options.D: The WiFi chip resets the date every time the program starts running

questions.explanation: The Pico counts seconds in an internal clock but has no battery to keep it running. When connected, Thonny sets the clock from your computer, but a power cycle with no computer leaves it at a default date in early 2021. The fix is a time source: a DS3231 real-time clock chip (Chapter 13) or WiFi time sync (Chapter 14).

questions.question_text: Why must you write `months[month - 1]` when looking up a month name in a list?

options.A: The tuple stores the months in reverse order
options.B: Month numbers start at 1, but list positions start at 0
options.C: The month field counts from zero, so January is 0
options.D: The list holds only eleven names, so one must be skipped

questions.explanation: The month field runs from 1 to 12, but a list is indexed from 0, so January sits at position 0 and December at position 11. Forgetting the subtraction is an off-by-one error that shows the wrong month, and in December it crashes with `IndexError`. The weekday needs no adjustment because it already starts at 0.

questions.question_text: What is the main difference between `sleep()` and checking `ticks_diff()` in a loop?

options.A: `sleep()` measures time of day, while `ticks_diff()` only counts seconds
options.B: `sleep()` works only on the Pico W, while `ticks_diff()` works on every board
options.C: `sleep()` blocks the program, while `ticks_diff()` lets it keep working while waiting
options.D: `sleep()` is accurate to a microsecond, while `ticks_diff()` is accurate to a second

questions.explanation: While a program is sleeping it does nothing else, so it cannot read a button or update a display. With `ticks_diff()`, the loop runs thousands of times per second and each pass asks whether enough time has passed, so other work continues. This shift from blocking to checking lets one Pico handle buttons, displays, and a clock at the same time.

questions.question_text: How should the 24-hour time 0:15 be shown in 12-hour format?
questions.explanation: Using `(hour + 11) % 12 + 1` with hour 0 gives 12, and because 0 is before noon the suffix is AM, so midnight is 12:15 AM. A 12-hour clock never shows 0. Noon, hour 12, also gives 12 but with PM. Clock bugs hide at these boundaries, so test hours 0, 11, 12, 13, and 23 by hand before trusting a conversion.

questions.question_text: How many seconds since midnight is the time 14:05:09?
questions.explanation: The formula is 3600 × hours + 60 × minutes + seconds. Here that is 3600 × 14 + 60 × 5 + 9, which equals 50,400 + 300 + 9 = 50,709. Reducing the time to one integer between 0 and 86,399 makes comparisons simple, such as checking whether the time has passed a 7:30 alarm. Option B just joins the digits together, which is not a count of seconds.

questions.question_text: A web service sends the Unix timestamp 1,800,000,000. What value represents the same moment on the Pico, whose epoch starts in 2000?
questions.explanation: A Unix timestamp counts from January 1, 1970, while the Pico counts from January 1, 2000, and the two differ by 946,684,800 seconds. Subtract that offset: 1,800,000,000 − 946,684,800 = 853,315,200. Adding the offset instead gives option A, and leaving the value alone gives option C, which would put your clock about 30 years off.

questions.question_text: Why can subtracting two `ticks_ms()` values with the `-` operator sometimes give a wrong or negative answer?

options.A: The counter holds only seconds, so milliseconds are lost in the subtraction
options.B: The counter resets to zero every time the program calls `sleep()`
options.C: The counter wraps back to zero after about 12.4 days, which `ticks_diff()` handles correctly
options.D: The counter counts down instead of up, so the result is always reversed

questions.explanation: The `ticks_ms()` counter is not endless. It wraps back to zero after 2^30 milliseconds, which is about 12.4 days. If the wrap falls between your two readings, plain subtraction gives a wrong, even negative, result. The `ticks_diff(new, old)` function subtracts correctly across the wrap, so always use it instead of `-` in timing code.

questions.question_text: A clock adds 1 to a seconds counter after each `sleep(1)` and slowly runs behind real time. What is the cause and the best fix?

options.A: Each pass takes slightly over one second, so the error grows; read the real time with `localtime()` each pass
options.B: The `sleep()` function wakes up early, so the fix is to call it twice per pass
options.C: The seconds counter overflows after 60, so the fix is to store it in a tuple
options.D: The display refreshes too often, so the fix is to remove the loop entirely

questions.explanation: The loop spends extra time running its other instructions, so each pass takes a little more than one second, and the error adds up with every tick. A better approach is to ask for the actual time on each pass, as the chapter's clock loop does with `localtime()`. Then `sleep(1)` only controls how often the screen is redrawn, not how time is counted.

questions.question_text: What is contact bounce?

options.A: A wiring mistake that happens when both legs are on the same side of the button
options.B: The delay Python adds between two quick presses of the same button
options.C: A burst of rapid on/off pulses as metal contacts collide and spring apart
options.D: A voltage drop that appears when the internal pull-up is turned on

questions.explanation: A mechanical switch is not a clean on/off device. When its contacts close they chatter for a few milliseconds up to about 20 ms before settling. A human sees one press, but the fast Pico can see the burst as ten presses. Debouncing is any technique that ignores the bounce so one physical press counts as exactly one event.

questions.question_text: Which trigger makes an interrupt handler run at the instant a pull-up button is pressed?

options.A: `Pin.IRQ_RISING`
options.B: `Pin.IRQ_FALLING`
options.C: `Pin.PULL_UP`
options.D: `Pin.OUT`

questions.explanation: A pull-up button is active low, so the pin goes from 1 to 0 when it is pressed. That change from high to low is a falling edge. `Pin.IRQ_RISING` would fire when the button is released, and you can combine both constants with the `|` operator to hear press and release. `Pin.PULL_UP` and `Pin.OUT` configure the pin and are not interrupt triggers.

questions.question_text: Why should an interrupt handler just set a flag instead of drawing on the display?

options.A: Flags are the only variables that a handler is allowed to read
options.B: Handlers cannot be attached to pins that also drive displays
options.C: Drawing code stops working when a button has a pull-up resistor
options.D: A handler must finish quickly, so the main loop should do the heavy work

questions.explanation: An interrupt handler pauses your main code, so it must be short and fast. Long work such as drawing or a `sleep()` call inside it causes trouble. The recommended pattern is to set `pressed = True` and return, then let the main loop notice the flag, clear it, and do the real work. This keeps handlers quick and your display code safe.

questions.question_text: A four-leg tactile switch never seems to work when it is wired using two legs on the same side. Why?

options.A: Legs on the same side are always joined, so pressing the button changes nothing between them
options.B: The button needs an external resistor on each of the two legs that are used
options.C: Tactile switches work only when all four legs are connected to a pin
options.D: The two legs on the same side are connected only while the button is held

questions.explanation: Inside the case, the four legs form two pairs, and the legs on the same side of each pair are always connected. Pressing the button joins the two pairs to each other. So a connection that uses two legs from the same pair will never see a change. Wire the button between a leg of one pair and a leg of the opposite pair, such as across the breadboard center gap.

questions.question_text: How can the same Mode button do different things in a clock with RUN, SET_HOUR, and SET_MINUTE?

options.A: Each state has its own wire connected to a different GPIO pin
options.B: What a press does depends on the state the program is currently in
options.C: The button changes its resistance each time it is pressed
options.D: The interrupt handler is replaced by a new one after every press

questions.explanation: A state machine organizes a program around named states, and each state defines what happens on an event. In RUN, a Mode press goes to SET_HOUR, and in SET_HOUR it goes to SET_MINUTE. The question to ask is "What state am I in, and what does this event do there?" That is how two buttons can control a whole clock interface.

questions.question_text: A software debounce window is 50 ms. A press was accepted at 1,000 ms. Later events arrive at 1,012 ms, 1,030 ms, and 1,200 ms. Which events are accepted?

options.A: Only the event at 1,012 ms
options.B: The events at 1,012 ms and 1,030 ms
options.C: Only the event at 1,200 ms
options.D: All three of the events

questions.explanation: The `ticks_diff(now, last_press) > 50` test rejects anything that arrives within 50 ms of the last accepted press. The events at 1,012 ms and 1,030 ms are only 12 ms and 30 ms later, so they are bounce and are ignored. The event at 1,200 ms is 200 ms later, so it counts as a new press. A window of 20 to 50 ms stops bounce but still feels instant.

questions.question_text: A clock uses `MODES = ["RUN", "SET_HOUR", "SET_MINUTE"]` and `mode = (mode + 1) % len(MODES)`. The current mode is SET_MINUTE. What happens when the Mode button is pressed?

options.A: The mode moves to SET_HOUR
options.B: The mode stays at SET_MINUTE
options.C: The program stops with an `IndexError`
options.D: The mode wraps back around to RUN

questions.explanation: SET_MINUTE is at index 2, so `(2 + 1) % 3` equals 0, which is the index of RUN. The modulo operator makes the mode wrap from the last state back to the first, and no index ever goes past the end of the list. After three presses from RUN you are back to RUN. The Cycle button uses the same wrap trick with `% 24` for hours and `% 60` for minutes.

questions.question_text: A 0.1 µF capacitor is placed across a button that uses the internal 50 kΩ pull-up. What is the time constant R × C?

options.A: About 5 ms
options.B: About 50 ms
options.C: About 0.5 ms
options.D: About 500 ms

questions.explanation: Multiply 50,000 Ω by 0.0000001 F to get 0.005 seconds, or 5 ms. That is on the same order as typical contact bounce, so the capacitor smooths the rapid changes with no extra code. This is hardware debouncing. In this course, software debouncing is more common because it needs no extra parts.

questions.question_text: A decoder runs on each falling edge of signal A and reads signal B at that moment. Why does reading B reveal the direction of rotation?

options.A: A and B are offset by a quarter cycle, so B has a different level at A's edge for each direction
options.B: B stays at 1 when the knob turns clockwise and at 0 when it turns counterclockwise
options.C: B counts the number of clicks while A measures the speed of the turn
options.D: A and B always change at exactly the same instant in either direction

questions.explanation: The two encoder switches produce a quadrature pattern in which A and B change in a fixed order, offset by a quarter of a cycle. Clockwise gives the sequence 00, 10, 11, 01, and counterclockwise gives it in reverse. So at a falling edge of A, B is high for one direction and low for the other. Swap the two directions if your knob feels backward.

questions.question_text: A time-setting program polls a button inside a loop that redraws the display and then sleeps for two seconds. Short presses are often missed. What is the best fix?

options.A: Add a larger capacitor across the button to stretch each press
options.B: Increase the debounce window to 500 ms so presses last longer
options.C: Attach an `irq()` handler on the falling edge that sets a flag for the main loop
options.D: Change the pull-up to a pull-down so the button reads 1 when pressed

questions.explanation: Polling only sees the pin when the loop asks, so a press that starts and ends during the two-second sleep is never noticed. An interrupt lets the hardware watch the pin and run a short handler the moment it changes, so no press is missed. The handler sets a flag, and the main loop does the work. A longer debounce window or a different pull does not help with missed presses.

questions.chapter: Communication Buses: I2C, SPI, and UART
questions.question_text: What is the typical I2C address of an SSD1306 OLED display?
questions.explanation: An SSD1306 OLED normally answers at `0x3C`, which is 60 in decimal. The DS3231 real-time clock uses `0x68`, the memory chip on RTC boards uses `0x57`, and the BME280 temperature sensor uses `0x76`. Every I2C message starts with the 7-bit address, and only the matching device pays attention to the rest of it.

questions.chapter: Communication Buses: I2C, SPI, and UART
questions.question_text: Which bit of a byte is the MSB?

options.A: The rightmost bit, which is worth 1
options.B: The leftmost bit, which is worth 128
options.C: The middle bit, which is worth 16
options.D: Whichever bit currently holds a 1

questions.explanation: The most significant bit is the leftmost bit of a byte and is worth 128, while the least significant bit is the rightmost and is worth 1. In `0b10110001` both the MSB and the LSB happen to be 1. Changing the MSB changes the value the most, and changing the LSB changes it the least. Bit ordering decides which of the two goes onto the wire first.

questions.chapter: Communication Buses: I2C, SPI, and UART
questions.question_text: Why do I2C lines need pull-up resistors?

options.A: Devices can only pull a wire down, so the resistors return it to 3.3 V
options.B: They slow the clock so that devices at different speeds stay in step
options.C: They give every device on the bus its own unique 7-bit address
options.D: They convert the 3.3 V signals into 5 V signals for the peripherals

questions.explanation: I2C lines are open-drain, meaning a device can pull a wire down to ground but never push it up. The pull-up resistors, commonly 4.7 kΩ, bring the wire back to 3.3 V. Most hobbyist modules already include them. The Pico's internal pull-ups of about 50 kΩ are too weak for reliable 400 kHz operation, so a missing pull-up is a prime suspect when a bus fails.

questions.chapter: Communication Buses: I2C, SPI, and UART
questions.question_text: How does SPI make sure only one peripheral listens when several share the same clock and data wires?

options.A: Each peripheral is given a unique 7-bit address at the start of every message
options.B: The controller changes the baudrate to a different value for each peripheral
options.C: The controller pulls one device's chip select low while the others stay high
options.D: Each peripheral takes turns based on the order in which it was plugged in

questions.explanation: SPI has no addresses. Each peripheral gets its own chip select (CS) wire. The controller pulls CS low to wake one device, and the devices whose CS stays high ignore the traffic. After the transfer, CS goes back high. This is why SPI needs one extra pin per device, while I2C devices share the same two signal wires.

questions.chapter: Communication Buses: I2C, SPI, and UART
questions.question_text: Why must a round color display use SPI instead of I2C?

options.A: I2C cannot carry color information on its two wires
options.B: SPI uses fewer wires than I2C and so costs less
options.C: Color displays have no I2C address, so the controller cannot find them
options.D: SPI moves far more data per second, sending a 240 by 240 frame in about 23 ms

questions.explanation: A 240 by 240 frame at 2 bytes per pixel is 115,200 bytes. At 40 MHz SPI that takes about 23 ms, but over I2C at 400 kHz it takes about 2.6 seconds, far too slow for animation. Small monochrome OLEDs have only 1,024 bytes to send, so I2C is fast enough for them. Speed, not color support or wire count, is the deciding factor.

questions.chapter: Communication Buses: I2C, SPI, and UART
questions.question_text: How should a Pico be connected to a GPS module over UART?

options.A: Pico TX to the module's RX, and Pico RX to the module's TX
options.B: Pico TX to the module's TX, and Pico RX to the module's RX
options.C: Pico TX and RX both to the module's single data pin
options.D: Pico TX to the module's clock pin, and Pico RX to ground

questions.explanation: UART uses two data wires, TX and RX, and the connection is crossed so that what one side transmits, the other receives. UART has no clock wire, so both ends must also agree in advance on a baud rate such as 9600 or 115200 bits per second. Connecting TX to TX leaves both devices talking and nobody listening.

questions.chapter: Communication Buses: I2C, SPI, and UART
questions.question_text: Which line sets bit 5 of the byte `x` without changing any of the other bits?

options.C: `x = x ^ 0xFF`

questions.explanation: The expression `1 << 5` makes a byte with only bit 5 set. OR-ing it with `x` turns that bit on and leaves every other bit as it was. The AND in option A would clear every other bit, XOR with `0xFF` flips all eight bits, and shifting right by 5 moves the whole byte instead of changing a single bit. Use `x & ~(1 << 5)` to clear a bit.

questions.chapter: Communication Buses: I2C, SPI, and UART
questions.question_text: In what order do the bits of `0xC1` (`0b11000001`) appear on the wire when sent LSB first?
questions.explanation: LSB-first order sends the rightmost bit first and the leftmost bit last, so the byte 11000001 is read from right to left as 1 0 0 0 0 0 1 1. Option A is the MSB-first order. Sender and receiver must agree on the order or every byte arrives scrambled. Most SPI displays use MSB first, which is the MicroPython default.

questions.chapter: Communication Buses: I2C, SPI, and UART
questions.question_text: An OLED and a DS3231 clock chip are both wired to the same SDA and SCL pins, but the scanner shows only `[60]`. What does this most strongly suggest?

options.A: The Pico's I2C pins are damaged and cannot find any device
options.B: The bus works, so the fault is in the clock chip's own power or wiring
options.C: Both devices use address 60, so the scanner lists them once
options.D: The scanner can detect only one device on a bus at a time

questions.explanation: The OLED at `0x3C` (60) answered, which proves the Pico's pins, the shared wires, and the pull-ups all work. The DS3231 should appear at `0x68` (104), so the problem is specific to that module: its power, its ground, or its own SDA and SCL connections. The scanner lists every address that answers, and two devices with the same address would conflict, not merge.

questions.chapter: Communication Buses: I2C, SPI, and UART
questions.question_text: A color display shows flickering pixels when the SPI baudrate is 40 MHz and 30 cm jumper wires are used. What is the best first step?

options.A: Add I2C pull-up resistors to the SPI clock and data wires
options.B: Switch the byte order from MSB first to LSB first
options.C: Hold the chip select wire low permanently to keep the display awake
options.D: Lower the baudrate and shorten the signal wires

questions.explanation: Long wires, loose connections, and very high speeds distort the signal edges, so the receiver may read a 0 as a 1. Shortening the wires and lowering the baudrate are the simplest fixes for signal integrity. Also check that grounds are shared and add a 0.1 µF capacitor near the chip's power pins. Pull-ups belong to I2C, and a wrong bit order would scramble the image rather than make pixels flicker.

questions.chapter: LED Displays and the First Digital Clock
questions.question_text: How many wires does a TM1637 four-digit display module need to connect to the Pico?

options.A: Two
options.B: Four
options.C: Eight
options.D: Twelve

questions.explanation: The TM1637 needs power, ground, and two signal wires called CLK and DIO. The driver chip does all the multiplexing for you. Wiring the digits directly would take about 12 pins, which is why the TM1637 module is the first clock display in this course. It costs only about one to two dollars.

questions.chapter: LED Displays and the First Digital Clock
questions.question_text: Which segment of a seven-segment digit is the one in the middle of the figure 8?

options.A: Segment a
options.B: Segment d
options.C: Segment g
options.D: Segment dp

questions.explanation: The segments are labeled `a` through `g`, starting at the top and going clockwise, with `g` in the middle. Segment `d` is the bottom bar, and `a` is the top bar. Many displays add an eighth dot, `dp`, for the decimal point. A program stores each digit as one byte with one bit per segment, so bit 6 controls segment `g`.

questions.chapter: LED Displays and the First Digital Clock
questions.question_text: How does segment multiplexing let a four-digit display work with only about 12 pins?

options.A: Only one digit is lit at a time, cycling so fast that persistence of vision makes all look lit
options.B: Each digit is wired to its own driver chip, which reduces the pin count
options.C: The segments are lit at only half brightness, so fewer wires are needed
options.D: The display remembers its pattern and no longer needs to be refreshed

questions.explanation: All four digits share the same 8 segment lines, and each digit has its own select wire, giving 8 + 4 = 12 pins. The controller lights one digit at a time, cycling more than 100 times per second, and persistence of vision blends them. The cost is that each digit is on only a quarter of the time, so each segment needs about four times the current, and something must keep cycling.

questions.chapter: LED Displays and the First Digital Clock
questions.question_text: A TM1637 is wired to GP2 and GP3, but an I2C scan finds nothing. Why?

options.A: The module must be broken, because every working module appears in the scan
options.B: The scanner only lists devices that use 5 V power
options.C: GP2 and GP3 are not allowed to be used with the TM1637
options.D: The TM1637 uses its own protocol with no device address, so a scan cannot find it

questions.explanation: The TM1637's CLK and DIO wires look like I2C, but it has its own protocol and no device address. That also means it can connect to any two GPIO pins. A scan that finds nothing does not prove the module is bad. To test it, run the driver library's `numbers()` call and look at the display instead of using the scanner.

questions.chapter: LED Displays and the First Digital Clock
questions.question_text: Why does a character LCD such as the LCD1602 need a backlight?

options.A: The backlight supplies the 5 V that the HD44780 chip needs to run
options.B: An LCD makes no light of its own and only blocks or passes light
options.C: The backlight refreshes the characters so they do not fade
options.D: Without a backlight the text appears in the wrong font

questions.explanation: Unlike an LED display, where each LED glows by itself, a liquid crystal display does not produce light. It blocks or passes light that already exists, so in the dark it needs a backlight to be readable. The LCD1602 has 16 columns and 2 rows and uses the HD44780 controller. An I2C backpack reduces its wiring from about 10 pins to four wires.

questions.chapter: LED Displays and the First Digital Clock
questions.question_text: Which segments are lit to show the digit 1, and what is its segment byte?

options.A: Segments a and b, with byte `0x03`
options.B: Segments e and f, with byte `0x30`
options.C: Segments b and c, with byte `0x06`
options.D: All seven segments, with byte `0x7F`

questions.explanation: The digit 1 uses the two right-hand bars, segments `b` and `c`. Bit 1 is segment `b` and bit 2 is segment `c`, so the byte is `0b00000110`, which is `0x06`. All seven segments lit with `0x7F` makes the digit 8. Remember that a 1 bit turns a segment on, which is the bit manipulation idea from Chapter 8 in action.

questions.chapter: LED Displays and the First Digital Clock
questions.question_text: A clock uses `tm.numbers(h, m, colon=(s % 2 == 0))`. What is the colon doing at 14:05:07?

options.A: Off, because 7 is odd and the test is false
options.B: On, because 7 is greater than zero
options.C: On, because the minute is odd
options.D: Off, because the colon only lights at the top of each minute

questions.explanation: The expression `s % 2 == 0` is true only for even seconds, so the colon is on for even seconds and off for odd ones. At second 7 the remainder is 1, the test is false, and the colon is off. Because the state comes from the real seconds value instead of a toggled variable, the blink can never get out of step with the time.

questions.chapter: LED Displays and the First Digital Clock
questions.question_text: You want to move a TM1637 to GP10 for CLK and GP11 for DIO. What do you need to do?

options.A: Nothing can be done, because the module only works on GP2 and GP3
options.B: Create the display with `I2C(0, sda=Pin(10), scl=Pin(11))` instead
options.C: Connect it to the SPI0 pins and set a baudrate for the display
options.D: Wire CLK and DIO to those pins and pass `Pin(10)` and `Pin(11)` to the constructor

questions.explanation: Since the TM1637 protocol has no address and no special hardware requirements, it works on any two GPIO pins. Wire the pins as you like, then create the object with `tm1637.TM1637(clk=Pin(10), dio=Pin(11))`. Update the wiring table or `config.py` too, so your documentation matches the build. Using the I2C or SPI classes would not work, because the TM1637 is neither.

questions.chapter: LED Displays and the First Digital Clock
questions.question_text: A bare multiplexed display freezes on one digit when the program pauses for five seconds, but a TM1637 module keeps showing all four digits. What explains the difference?

options.A: The TM1637 uses larger LEDs that glow even after power is removed
options.B: The TM1637 lights all four digits at the same time instead of multiplexing
options.C: The TM1637 chip does the cycling by itself, so the program does not need to
options.D: The TM1637 stores the digits in the Pico's flash memory

questions.explanation: Multiplexing demands that something keeps cycling through the digits constantly. If your own program does that and then stops to do other work, the display flickers or freezes on one digit. The TM1637 driver chip handles the multiplexing internally. You send it the digits once and it keeps them lit, which leaves your program free to sleep or do other tasks.

questions.chapter: LED Displays and the First Digital Clock
questions.question_text: Why is it risky to connect an LCD1602 with an I2C backpack straight to the Pico's SDA and SCL pins?

options.A: The LCD1602 uses SPI, so I2C pins can never carry its signals
options.B: Many backpacks pull the lines up to 5 V, which can damage the Pico's 3.3 V pins
options.C: The backpack address of `0x27` is reserved for the Pico itself
options.D: The backlight drains so much current that the pins burn out

questions.explanation: LCD1602 modules normally run on 5 V, and many backpacks include pull-up resistors that raise SDA and SCL to 5 V. The Pico's GPIO pins are only 3.3 V tolerant, so this can send 5 V into them and cause damage. Use a level shifter or a module with 3.3 V pull-ups, as you learned in Chapter 2. The backpack normally appears at `0x27` or `0x3F` on the scanner.

questions.question_text: Where is the origin (0, 0) on a display's coordinate system?

options.A: At the bottom-left corner of the screen
options.B: At the center of the screen
options.C: At the top-left corner of the screen
options.D: At the top-right corner of the screen

questions.explanation: On a display, x is the column counted from the left and y is the row counted from the top, so the origin is the top-left pixel. On a 240 by 240 screen the bottom-right pixel is (239, 239). This differs from a math class graph, where the origin is at the bottom-left and y increases upward. A point that looks higher on the screen has a smaller y.

questions.question_text: What unit of angle do MicroPython's `math.sin()` and `math.cos()` expect?

options.A: Radians
options.B: Degrees
options.C: Clock positions from 0 to 59
options.D: Pixels along the arc

questions.explanation: Like most programming languages, MicroPython's math functions work in radians, where a full circle is about 6.283. Use `math.radians()` to convert from degrees. Passing a degree value directly gives an answer, but the wrong one, which makes this a classic mistake. Degrees, which split a circle into 360 parts, are what people use when thinking about angles.

questions.question_text: Why does the formula for the screen position of a clock hand tip subtract the cosine term, as in `y = cy - r * cos(θ)`?

options.A: Cosine always returns a negative number for clock angles
options.B: Subtraction keeps the result inside the display's pixel range
options.C: The hand length must be reduced as the angle increases
options.D: The screen's y-axis points down, so moving up means a smaller y

questions.explanation: Clock angles start at 12 o'clock and go clockwise. At 0 degrees the tip should be straight above the center, which on the screen means a smaller y value. Because screen y increases downward, the cosine term is subtracted. Sine goes with x, since at 3 o'clock the tip moves right by the full radius. This pair of lines places every hand, tick mark, and number on a round face.

questions.question_text: Why does the hour hand angle formula include the extra term `0.5 * m`?

options.A: It converts the hour from 24-hour form to 12-hour form
options.B: It lets the hand creep smoothly instead of jumping from one hour to the next
options.C: It adds the angle of the second hand to the hour hand
options.D: It keeps the hour hand shorter than the minute hand

questions.explanation: The hour hand turns 30 degrees per hour, which is 0.5 degrees per minute. Adding `0.5 * m` moves it a little each minute. Without it, the hand would sit exactly on the 3 until it jumped to the 4 on the hour, which looks wrong at 3:59. The conversion from 24-hour form is done by `h % 12`, and hand length is a separate matter.

questions.question_text: Why is it better to write each hand length as a fraction of the face radius than as a fixed number of pixels?

options.A: The design scales automatically to any display size
options.B: The Pico can only draw lines whose length is less than one
options.C: Fractions are drawn faster than whole numbers on the screen
options.D: The hour, minute, and second hands must all have the same length

questions.explanation: If the hour hand is 0.50 of the radius, the minute hand 0.75, and the second hand 0.90, the same program works on a 240 pixel face or a 360 pixel face with no changes. Fixed pixel lengths would need editing for every screen. The hands also have different lengths on purpose, so you can tell them apart at a glance.

questions.question_text: What is the angle of the hour hand at 9:15:00, using `30 * (h % 12) + 0.5 * m`?

options.A: 270 degrees
options.B: 285 degrees
options.C: 277.5 degrees
options.D: 315 degrees

questions.explanation: The hour part is 30 × 9 = 270 degrees, and the minute part is 0.5 × 15 = 7.5 degrees, for a total of 277.5. The hour hand has moved a quarter of the way from the 9 toward the 10. The minute hand at that time is at 6 × 15 = 90 degrees, pointing at the 3. A value of exactly 270 would ignore the minutes.

questions.question_text: A hand of length 100 starts at the center (120, 120) and points at 6 o'clock, which is 180 degrees. Where is its tip?
questions.explanation: At 180 degrees, sine is 0 and cosine is −1, so x = 120 + 100 × 0 = 120 and y = 120 − 100 × (−1) = 220. The tip is straight below the center, which is correct for 6 o'clock because y grows downward. Option A is the 3 o'clock position, option B is 12 o'clock, and option C is 9 o'clock.

questions.question_text: A fixed-point lookup table uses `SCALE = 256`. Which integer is stored for the sine of 30 degrees?
questions.explanation: The sine of 30 degrees is 0.5, and multiplying by the scale factor of 256 gives 128. To get the real value back, you divide by 256 or shift right by 8. Storing sine and cosine for the 60 possible angles at startup means each frame needs only integer multiplication and shifts. A stored value of 256 would stand for a sine of 1, which happens at 90 degrees.

questions.question_text: A student's clock draws the hand pointing straight down at 12:00, and straight up at 6:00. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The angle was left in degrees instead of being changed to radians
options.B: The center point was calculated with `/` instead of `//`
options.C: The student added `r * cos(θ)` to `cy` instead of subtracting it
options.D: The hand length was set larger than the radius of the face

questions.explanation: Adding the cosine term instead of subtracting it flips the vertical direction, because the screen's y-axis points down. The hand then points in exactly the opposite vertical direction, as if the math-class convention had been used. A degree-versus-radian error would produce hands pointing in seemingly random directions, not a clean mirror image, and an oversized length would only make the hand too long.

questions.question_text: Why does a lookup table with fixed-point integers speed up drawing an analog face on the RP2040?

options.A: The RP2040 has no floating-point hardware, so a precomputed table avoids slow software sine and cosine
options.B: The table lets the Pico skip the drawing step for the tick marks entirely
options.C: Integers use less flash memory than floats, so programs load faster
options.D: The RP2040 can only perform sine and cosine on whole-number angles

questions.explanation: Every `sin()` and `cos()` call on the RP2040 runs in software, which is relatively slow, and calling them for 60 tick marks each frame wastes time. Computing the values once at startup and storing them as scaled integers means each frame needs only multiplication and bit shifts. The rounding error is at most 1/256 of the length, less than half a pixel for a 120-pixel hand.

questions.question_text: How many bytes of RAM does a framebuffer for a 128 × 64 monochrome OLED need?

options.A: 1,024 bytes
options.B: 8,192 bytes
options.C: 128 bytes
options.D: 64 bytes

questions.explanation: A monochrome pixel needs 1 bit, so the memory is 128 × 64 × 1 / 8 = 1,024 bytes. The value 8,192 is the number of pixels, not bytes, since eight pixels share each byte. This small buffer is why the OLED can keep a full copy of its screen in RAM, while large color displays sometimes cannot.

questions.question_text: Which call copies the framebuffer to the OLED so that the picture becomes visible?

options.A: `oled.fill(0)`
options.B: `oled.pixel(x, y, 1)`
options.C: `oled.text("Hi", 0, 0)`
options.D: `oled.show()`

questions.explanation: Drawing calls such as `fill()`, `pixel()`, and `text()` change only the framebuffer in RAM. Nothing appears on the panel until `show()` sends the buffer across the bus. A blank OLED very often means the `show()` call is missing. Every frame should end with exactly one `show()`, after the buffer has been cleared and all drawing is done.

questions.question_text: What is the main benefit of drawing into a framebuffer first and then calling `show()`?

options.A: The framebuffer makes the OLED panel brighter than direct drawing
options.B: Viewers never see half-drawn frames because the whole picture appears at once
options.C: The framebuffer removes the need to wire a bus to the display
options.D: Drawing into memory uses no RAM, so the Pico saves energy

questions.explanation: A framebuffer is a block of RAM holding a copy of every pixel. You can draw a hundred things in it, and then one fast transfer shows them all at the same instant, like a painter who finishes a canvas behind a curtain. The design avoids flicker and keeps drawing code simple. The cost is the RAM, which is only 1,024 bytes for this OLED.

questions.question_text: A 1.3-inch OLED shows its image shifted about two pixels to the side, with garbage at the edge, when using the SSD1306 driver. What is the likely cause?

options.A: The I2C address was set to `0x3D` instead of `0x3C`
options.B: The framebuffer was never cleared with `fill(0)`
options.C: The module has an SH1106 controller whose memory is 132 columns wide
options.D: The baudrate was set too high for the SPI bus

questions.explanation: The SH1106 controller looks the same and uses the same wiring, but its memory is 132 columns wide instead of 128. The SSD1306 driver therefore puts the picture two pixels off. The fix is the `sh1106.py` driver, which has the same methods. Check the controller name in the product listing before you buy. A wrong address or baudrate would give a blank or garbled screen, not a clean shift.

questions.question_text: Why should you call `show()` once per frame rather than after every drawing call?

options.A: The OLED can only accept one command per second
options.B: Calling `show()` more than once erases the framebuffer
options.C: The driver ignores any drawing done after the first `show()`
options.D: It is the slowest step because it moves the whole buffer over the bus

questions.explanation: The `show()` call transfers all 1,024 bytes across I2C or SPI, which is the slowest step in your drawing code. Calling it after every line multiplies that cost for no benefit. Do all your drawing first and reveal the finished frame once. The routine for every frame is to clear, draw everything, and then show.

questions.question_text: How much memory does a 360 × 360 color display need at 16 bits per pixel?

options.A: 259,200 bytes
options.B: 129,600 bytes
options.C: 16,200 bytes

questions.explanation: Use memory = W × H × bpp / 8, which gives 360 × 360 × 16 / 8 = 259,200 bytes. That is almost the entire 264 KB of RAM on the Pico, which explains why large color displays often cannot keep a full framebuffer. Option B counts two bytes fewer per pixel, option C divides the pixel count by eight, and option D forgets to divide by 8 bits per byte.

questions.question_text: On a 128-wide `MONO_VLSB` buffer, which byte index and bit hold the pixel at (50, 13)?

options.A: Index 63, bit 5
options.B: Index 178, bit 5
options.C: Index 178, bit 1
options.D: Index 306, bit 5

questions.explanation: The formula is index = x + floor(y / 8) × width, and bit = y mod 8. Here y = 13 gives page 1 and bit 5, so the index is 50 + 1 × 128 = 178. Option A simply adds x and y, option C confuses the page with the bit, and option D uses page 2 by mistake. You never compute this by hand because `pixel()` does it for you.

questions.question_text: About how long does one `show()` take to send the 1,024-byte OLED buffer over I2C at 400 kHz, using 9 clock cycles per byte?

options.A: About 0.8 ms
options.B: About 2.3 ms
options.C: About 23 ms
options.D: About 230 ms

questions.explanation: The time is 1,024 × 9 / 400,000, which is about 0.023 seconds, or 23 ms. That allows up to roughly 43 frames per second, which is plenty for a clock that changes once per second. The 0.8 ms figure belongs to SPI at 10 MHz. You can measure the real time with `ticks_us()` and `ticks_diff()`.

questions.question_text: A counter program draws a new number each second, but the digits pile up into an unreadable blob. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The `fill(0)` call is missing, so each number is drawn over the old one
options.B: The `show()` call is missing, so the screen never updates at all
options.C: The baudrate is too low, so the digits arrive out of order
options.D: The display is an SH1106, so the digits draw in the wrong place

questions.explanation: Without clearing, each new value is drawn on top of the previous one in the framebuffer, so overlapping digits smear together. The routine for each frame is always `fill(0)`, then draw, then `show()`. If `show()` were missing, the screen would not update at all, rather than showing overlapping digits, so the clearing step is the one to check first.

questions.question_text: In a baudrate test, the picture is clean at 4 MHz and 8 MHz but garbled at 10 MHz. What speed should the final program use?

options.A: 10 MHz, because it is the fastest speed that was tried
options.B: About 8 MHz, which is safely below the first speed that showed errors
options.C: 20 MHz, because faster speeds always work after a warm-up
options.D: 1 MHz, because no display is reliable at higher speeds

questions.explanation: The recommended procedure is to find the first speed that shows errors, here 10 MHz, and then use a value about 20 to 30 percent below it, which is roughly 7 to 8 MHz. That margin matters because a setup that works on your desk can fail with longer wires or a warmer chip. Using the failing speed, or a faster one, would risk garbled pixels.

questions.question_text: In the call `rect(x, y, w, h, c)`, what do the third and fourth arguments mean?

options.A: The x and y position of the second corner of the rectangle
options.B: The horizontal and vertical radii of the rectangle
options.C: The color of the outline and a flag that fills the rectangle
options.D: The width and height of the rectangle

questions.explanation: A rectangle takes its top-left corner followed by a width and a height, not a second corner. So `rect(10, 10, 50, 30, 1)` draws a box 50 wide and 30 tall that ends at (59, 39). Mixing up size with a second corner is the most common shape bug, and the giveaway is a rectangle that is too big or too small by exactly the starting offset.

questions.question_text: How wide in pixels is the string `"09:45"` drawn with the built-in `text()` method at normal size?

options.A: 5 pixels
options.B: 40 pixels
options.C: 45 pixels
options.D: 80 pixels

questions.explanation: The built-in font uses an 8 by 8 pixel cell for every character, so the width is `8 * len(string)`. The string has 5 characters, giving 8 × 5 = 40 pixels. That means 16 characters fit across the 128-pixel OLED. Because the width is so predictable, you can center text with `x = (128 - 8 * len(msg)) // 2`.

questions.question_text: Why does `oled.ellipse(64, 32, 31, 31, 1)` draw a circle centered on a 128 × 64 screen?

options.A: The first two numbers are the top-left corner, and the last two are the screen size
options.B: The `ellipse` method always draws a circle no matter what radii are given
options.C: Equal radii make a circle, and (64, 32) is the center of the shape and of the screen
options.D: The value 31 is the diameter, so the circle fills the entire screen height

questions.explanation: The `ellipse(x, y, xr, yr, c)` call takes the center of the shape and the horizontal and vertical radii.
