When both radii are 31, the shape is a circle, and the point (64, 32) is the middle of a 128 by 64 screen. A radius of 31 fits the 64-pixel height. Unlike rectangles, an ellipse is positioned by its center, not its corner.

questions.question_text: What is the benefit of drawing a clock face into a second buffer and copying it with `blit()` each frame?

options.A: The unchanging parts are drawn once, so each frame only adds the moving hands
options.B: The second buffer makes the OLED panel brighter and sharper
options.C: The `blit()` call sends the picture to the display without needing `show()`
options.D: It removes the need to clear the screen at the start of each frame

questions.explanation: A second buffer holds the parts that never change, such as the tick marks. Each frame you copy that ready-made face into the main buffer with `blit()` and draw only the hands on top. This saves the time of redrawing 60 ticks every second. You still have to call `show()` to send the finished frame to the display.

questions.question_text: On the OLED, what does a partial screen update save, and what does it not save?

options.A: It saves bus time, but drawing still takes the same time
options.B: It saves both drawing time and bus time, because only the changed bytes are sent
options.C: It saves drawing time, but `show()` still sends the entire 1,024-byte buffer
options.D: It saves nothing, because the whole screen must be redrawn to change a digit

questions.explanation: With the OLED's framebuffer, you can erase and redraw only the region that changed, which saves drawing time. But `show()` still transfers the whole 1,024 bytes, so the bus time stays the same. On larger color displays, whose drivers can send just a window of pixels, a partial update also cuts the bus time a great deal.

questions.question_text: A student draws `09:45` with scaled digits at `scale = 4` on a 128-pixel-wide OLED. What happens?

options.A: The time fits exactly because 128 divided by 4 is 32
options.B: The width is 160 pixels, so it does not fit and a scale of 3 is needed
options.C: The digits shrink automatically to fit the screen width
options.D: The width is 80 pixels, so there is room left for the date

questions.explanation: Each character is 8 pixels wide before scaling, so the width is 8 × scale × the number of characters. For five characters at scale 4, that is 8 × 4 × 5 = 160 pixels, which is wider than the 128-pixel screen. At scale 3 the width is 120 pixels, which fits. Nothing resizes the digits for you, so check the width before choosing a scale.

questions.question_text: Which tuple is the bounding box `(x, y, w, h)` of the text `"12:34"` drawn at (80, 40) with the built-in font?
questions.explanation: The bounding box is the smallest rectangle that encloses the object. The text starts at (80, 40), is 8 × 5 = 40 pixels wide, and is 8 pixels tall. That gives (80, 40, 40, 8). With this box you can erase the old text exactly using `fill_rect(*box, 0)` and then draw the new value, which is the core of a partial update.

questions.question_text: Which call draws a filled rectangle 40 pixels wide and 10 pixels tall with its top-left corner at (20, 30)?
questions.explanation: The `fill_rect(x, y, w, h, c)` call takes the top-left corner, then the width and height, then the color, where 1 means on. Option B treats the numbers as a second corner, option C swaps the order of the arguments, and option D draws only an outline in the off color, which would erase pixels instead of lighting them.

questions.question_text: A scrolling message must stay inside a 40 × 8 area and not spill onto other parts of the screen. How can you clip it with `framebuf`?

options.A: Call `hline()` and `vline()` around the area to block the extra text
options.B: Draw into a small buffer the size of the region, then `blit()` it into place
options.C: Use a smaller font so the message never reaches the edge of the area
options.D: Call `show()` twice so that the extra pixels are overwritten

questions.explanation: The `framebuf` module clips only at the edges of the whole buffer, so it has no built-in smaller clipping rectangle. Drawing into a small buffer the size of the region discards anything that falls outside it automatically, and `blit()` then copies the buffer into place on the main screen. Lines drawn around the area would not hide text, and `show()` cannot erase pixels.

questions.question_text: A program raises a `MemoryError` after importing six large font modules. What is the best analysis and fix?

options.A: The fonts are written in the wrong language, so convert them to C
options.B: The OLED cannot display more than one font, so remove all but one
options.C: Each font module uses flash and RAM, so include only needed characters and limit the number of fonts
options.D: The Pico needs a faster baudrate to load that many fonts at once

questions.explanation: A loaded font is stored as Python data, so each module takes flash space and RAM when imported, and big fonts with many characters can use tens of kilobytes. The `font_to_py.py` option `-c 0123456789:` keeps the output small by including only the digits and colon. Two or three fonts is a practical ceiling on the Pico, which has 264 KB of RAM.

questions.question_text: At which I2C address does the DS3231 real-time clock answer?
questions.explanation: The DS3231 answers at `0x68`, which is 104 in decimal, and the address cannot be changed. An I2C scan that shows `[104]` proves the chip is wired correctly, and sharing the bus with an OLED gives `[60, 104]`. The address `0x3C` belongs to the OLED, `0x57` to the memory chip found on many RTC modules, and `0x76` to the BME280 sensor.

questions.question_text: How is the decimal number 45 stored in BCD format?
questions.explanation: BCD stores each decimal digit in its own four-bit nibble. The digit 4 becomes `0100` and the digit 5 becomes `0101`, giving `0100 0101`, which is written `0x45`. Option A is ordinary binary for 45. Reading the BCD byte as a plain integer would give 69, which is why a conversion function is needed.

questions.question_text: Why is timekeeping moved out of the Pico and into a separate RTC chip?

options.A: The chip has its own battery, so the time survives crashes and power loss
options.B: The Pico cannot count seconds at all without help from another chip
options.C: The RTC chip displays the time on the screen for the Pico
options.D: The RTC chip lets the Pico run at a faster processor speed

questions.explanation: A microcontroller is busy and can be turned off, but a timekeeper must never stop. The RTC has its own crystal and a connection for a backup battery, so it keeps counting when the main power is off, and the Pico simply asks it for the time over I2C. The Pico can count seconds on its own, but its internal clock has no battery and forgets the time at power-off.

questions.question_text: How does the DS3231 achieve its high accuracy compared with an ordinary crystal?

options.A: It uses a larger crystal that vibrates at a much higher frequency
options.B: It is synchronized to an internet time server every few seconds
options.C: It measures its own temperature and adjusts the crystal frequency every 64 seconds
options.D: It stores the time in BCD, which removes rounding errors

questions.explanation: Quartz crystals change frequency slightly as the temperature changes. The DS3231 is a temperature-compensated crystal oscillator: it measures the chip's temperature and corrects the frequency every 64 seconds. That keeps it within ±2 ppm from 0 to 40 °C, about 15 times better than the plain crystal on the Pico. It has no internet connection, and BCD affects only how numbers are stored.

questions.question_text: A clock runs exactly 3 seconds fast, but its ticks are perfectly steady. How is it best described?

options.A: Accurate and precise
options.B: Precise but not accurate
options.C: Accurate but not precise
options.D: Neither accurate nor precise

questions.explanation: Accuracy means the clock shows the right time, while precision means its ticks are consistent and repeatable. A clock that is steadily 3 seconds ahead does not show the right time, so it is not accurate, but its steady ticks make it precise. The DS3231 is both, because its drift is small and steady. Resolution is a separate idea, and an RTC's resolution is one second.

questions.question_text: The DS3231 seconds register contains the byte `0x27`. How many seconds does it represent?
questions.explanation: In BCD the high nibble is the tens digit and the low nibble is the ones digit, so `0x27` means 2 tens and 7 ones, which is 27. The function `bcd_to_dec(b)` computes `(b >> 4) * 10 + (b & 0x0F)` to do this. Reading the byte as an ordinary integer would give 39, because `0x27` is 39 in plain binary.

questions.question_text: To set the seconds to 38, which byte does `dec_to_bcd(38)` produce?
questions.explanation: The function computes `((38 // 10) << 4) | (38 % 10)`. The tens digit 3 shifted left four bits gives `0x30`, and OR-ing in the ones digit 8 gives `0x38`. Option A, `0x26`, is just 38 written in ordinary hexadecimal, which the chip would read as 26 seconds. The nibbles must hold the decimal digits themselves.

questions.question_text: Using drift = ppm × elapsed seconds / 1,000,000, about how many seconds can a ±20 ppm DS1307 drift in one day?

options.A: About 1.7 seconds
options.B: About 0.17 seconds
options.C: About 17 seconds
options.D: About 2.6 seconds

questions.explanation: One day has 86,400 seconds, so the drift is 20 × 86,400 / 1,000,000, which is about 1.7 seconds. The 0.17 second figure belongs to the DS3231 at ±2 ppm, and the 2.6 second figure belongs to the Pico's ±30 ppm crystal. Over a month the DS1307 can drift about 52 seconds, while the DS3231 drifts only about 5.

questions.question_text: A program reads the DS3231 seconds register with `readfrom_mem` and gets 48, but the true time is 30 seconds. What explains this?

options.A: The RTC is running 18 seconds fast and needs to be reset
options.B: The byte is BCD `0x30`, which is 48 when read as an ordinary integer
options.C: The program read the temperature register instead of the seconds
options.D: The chip stores seconds in hexadecimal, so 30 appears as 48

questions.explanation: The RTC stores 30 as BCD, with the digit 3 in the high nibble and 0 in the low nibble, which is the byte `0x30`. Read as an ordinary integer, `0x30` is 48. Passing the byte through `bcd_to_dec()` gives the right value. A drift of 18 seconds would not show up so neatly, and the temperature lives in registers `0x11` and `0x12`.

questions.question_text: A DS3231 module holds a non-rechargeable CR2032 cell, and the battery feels warm. What is the likely cause and the right action?

options.A: This is normal, because the RTC chip heats the cell as it counts time
options.B: The Pico is sending 5 V into the cell, so a 5 V battery should be fitted
options.C: The module has a charging circuit made for LIR2032 cells, so use that type or remove the charging resistor
options.D: The cell is too weak to run the chip, so a larger coin cell should be used

questions.explanation: Many cheap DS3231 modules include a small charging circuit meant for rechargeable LIR2032 batteries. Charging a non-rechargeable CR2032 can make it hot or cause it to leak. Install an LIR2032, or remove the charging resistor from the module, and never leave a suspiciously warm battery in place. The chip itself draws only a few microamps and does not warm the cell.

questions.question_text: The timestamp in an NTP server's reply counts seconds from which starting date?

options.A: January 1, 1970
options.B: January 1, 2000
options.C: January 1, 1900
options.D: January 1, 1980

questions.explanation: NTP counts from January 1, 1900. That is a third epoch beside the Unix epoch of 1970 and the MicroPython-on-the-Pico epoch of 2000. The `ntptime` library subtracts 3,155,673,600 seconds, the gap between 1900 and 2000, so you rarely handle this yourself. It does explain why raw NTP numbers look strange.

questions.question_text: Which WiFi band can the Pico W connect to?

options.A: 2.4 GHz only
options.B: 5 GHz only
options.C: Both 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz
options.D: Neither, because it supports only Bluetooth

questions.explanation: The Pico W supports 2.4 GHz WiFi only. If your network name exists only on the 5 GHz band, the Pico cannot see it. Networks that need a sign-in page or enterprise login also will not work directly. Ask your teacher for a compatible or guest network. The plain Pico has no wireless chip at all.

questions.question_text: Why is it recommended to keep the clock's internal time in UTC and convert to local time only when showing it?

options.A: UTC time is always shorter to store than local time
options.B: The Pico cannot store any time that has a time zone offset
options.C: UTC removes the need to ever sync with an NTP server
options.D: UTC is the same everywhere and ignores daylight saving, so changing zones changes one number

questions.explanation: UTC is the same everywhere at any instant and does not change for daylight saving. If you store and compare times in UTC and convert only in the last step before drawing digits, moving the clock to another time zone or handling daylight saving changes one number in one place. The rule is to store and compare in UTC and convert to local time when showing it to a person.

questions.question_text: Why should WiFi credentials be kept in a separate `secrets.py` file that is listed in `.gitignore`?

options.A: Python cannot connect to WiFi unless the password is in its own file
options.B: It keeps the password out of code that may be shared or uploaded publicly
options.C: It makes the WiFi connection faster than typing the password in `main.py`
options.D: It lets the Pico use a 5 GHz network instead of 2.4 GHz

questions.explanation: If you commit your password to a public Git repository, anyone can read it, and bots really do scan for such files. Keeping the SSID and password in `secrets.py` and adding it to `.gitignore` keeps them private. Commit a `secrets_example.py` with fake values so classmates know what to fill in. The separate file has no effect on connection speed or band.

questions.question_text: A clock shows the right time while connected to Thonny but is several hours off when it runs alone. What explains this?

options.A: The WiFi chip adds a random offset to the time every few hours
options.B: Thonny stores the correct time in flash, and unplugging erases it
options.C: Thonny sets the Pico's clock to your computer's local time, while `ntptime` sets it to UTC
options.D: The Pico loses its DNS server as soon as the USB cable is removed

questions.explanation: When Thonny connects, it sets the Pico's internal clock to your computer's local time. The `ntptime` library sets the same clock to UTC. A program written while connected to Thonny can therefore be off by the time zone offset when it runs alone. Pick one convention, preferably UTC inside with conversion for display, and test the program with Thonny unplugged.

questions.question_text: It is 02:40 UTC on the 10th. What is the local time in US Central Standard Time (UTC−6)?

options.A: 20:40 on the 9th
options.B: 08:40 on the 10th
options.C: 20:40 on the 10th
options.D: 02:40 on the 9th

questions.explanation: Add the offset of −6 hours to 02:40 on the 10th. Going back six hours crosses midnight, so the local time is 20:40 on the previous day, the 9th. Because the conversion is done on a count of seconds, MicroPython carries the date back correctly without extra code. Option B wrongly adds six hours, and options C and D forget to change the date or the hour.

questions.question_text: A clock is 2 seconds fast after 5 days (432,000 seconds). What is its drift?

options.A: About 0.46 ppm
options.B: About 2.0 ppm
options.C: About 46 ppm
options.D: About 4.6 ppm

questions.explanation: Drift in ppm is the error divided by the elapsed time, times one million: 2 / 432,000 × 1,000,000 is about 4.6 ppm. That is a little worse than a DS3231 at room temperature. Measuring drift over several days like this is the first step in calibrating a clock, which is useful for an offline DS3231 clock that must be very accurate.

questions.question_text: A clock drifts at 20 ppm and you can tolerate 0.5 seconds of error. About how often must it resynchronize?

options.A: About every hour
options.B: About every 7 hours
options.C: About every 24 hours
options.D: About every 3 days

questions.explanation: The sync interval is the tolerated error divided by the drift rate. A drift of 20 ppm is 0.00002 seconds per second, so 0.5 / 0.00002 equals 25,000 seconds, which is about 7 hours. Syncing every hour is more often than needed, and syncing once a day or every three days would allow errors well above the 0.5 second limit.

questions.question_text: At startup, `ntptime.settime()` raises an `OSError` because the router is slow to answer. What is the best design?

options.A: Let the program crash so the user restarts the Pico
options.B: Remove the NTP code and set the time by hand every day
options.C: Wrap the call in `try/except`, retry a few times, then keep running and try again later
options.D: Call `ntptime.settime()` in a tight loop until it works

questions.explanation: WiFi and NTP fail sometimes for ordinary reasons. A `try/except OSError` block with a few retries and a short sleep between them handles the failure. If it still fails, the clock should keep running on its own time and try again later. A clock that keeps ticking is better than one that stops to argue with the router, and hammering a shared server in a tight loop is impolite.

questions.question_text: A wall clock has no WiFi and must stay within about one minute per year. Which time source is the best choice?

options.A: A DS3231 with a coin-cell backup, which drifts about 5 seconds per month
options.B: The Pico's internal RTC, which drifts about 16 minutes per year
options.C: Thonny time sync, which sets the clock whenever the Pico loses power
options.D: NTP over WiFi, which gives millisecond accuracy with no network

questions.explanation: A DS3231 at about 2 ppm drifts roughly 5 seconds a month, which is about one minute a year, and its battery lets it survive power-off. The internal RTC at 30 ppm drifts around 16 minutes a year and forgets the time at power-off. Thonny sync needs a computer over USB, and NTP needs WiFi, which this clock does not have.

questions.question_text: How many bits does the RGB565 format use for red, green, and blue, in that order?

options.A: 5 bits, 6 bits, and 5 bits
options.B: 6 bits, 5 bits, and 5 bits
options.C: 8 bits, 8 bits, and 8 bits
options.D: 4 bits, 4 bits, and 4 bits

questions.explanation: RGB565 packs a color into 16 bits: 5 for red, 6 for green, and 5 for blue. That gives 32 × 64 × 32 = 65,536 possible colors, and each pixel takes exactly 2 bytes. A standard true color image uses 8 bits per channel, or 24 bits per pixel, so RGB565 cuts the memory by a third at the cost of slightly less smooth gradients.

questions.question_text: Which RGB565 value represents pure red?

options.D: `0xFFFF`

questions.explanation: Red occupies the top five bits of the 16-bit value, so full red is `0xF800`. Pure blue, in the lowest five bits, is `0x001F`, and pure green, in the middle six bits, is `0x07E0`. The value `0xFFFF` has every bit set, which is white. Black is `0x0000`. These values are worth memorizing.

questions.question_text: Why does RGB565 give the extra bit to green instead of red or blue?

options.A: Green pixels use more power, so they need finer control
options.B: The human eye is most sensitive to green, so extra detail there is most noticeable
options.C: Green is the only color that most displays can produce at full brightness
options.D: The `color565()` function needs one spare bit to mark the green channel

questions.explanation: The eye notices small changes in green more easily than in red or blue, so giving green 6 bits (64 levels) while red and blue get 5 bits (32 levels) makes the best use of only 16 bits per pixel. The `color565()` function keeps the top 5 or 6 bits of each 0 to 255 channel value and shifts them into their places.

questions.question_text: Why does the 360 × 360 GC9B72 display draw directly instead of using a framebuffer with `show()`?

options.A: Direct writing makes the colors brighter than a framebuffer would
options.B: The GC9B72 chip cannot store any pixel colors of its own
options.C: SPI displays are not able to receive a whole frame at once
options.D: A full framebuffer needs 259,200 bytes, nearly all of the Pico's 264 KB of RAM

questions.explanation: At 2 bytes per pixel, 360 × 360 pixels need 259,200 bytes, leaving almost no room for anything else. A direct write display sends pixels straight to the display's own memory, so every call such as `fill_rect()` or `text()` changes the glass at once and there is no `show()`. The cost is that you must draw static parts once and update only what changed.

questions.question_text: Why is an IPS panel the better choice for a wearable watch display?

options.A: You rarely look at a wrist straight-on, and IPS keeps its colors at wide angles
options.B: IPS panels need no backlight, so a watch battery lasts longer
options.C: IPS panels have a contrast ratio of exactly 21 to 1
options.D: IPS panels use a framebuffer, which keeps the picture from flickering

questions.explanation: Viewing angle is how far off-center you can look before the colors wash out or invert. IPS panels, common on round watch displays, hold their colors to about 160 degrees or more, while older, cheaper TN panels fade quickly when viewed from above or below. Because a wrist watch is always glanced at from an angle, a wide viewing angle matters. IPS panels still need a backlight.

questions.question_text: A round display has a safe radius of 168 pixels. About how wide is the usable row 140 pixels above the center, using w = 2√(R² − d²)?

options.A: About 336 pixels
options.B: About 56 pixels
options.C: About 186 pixels
options.D: About 280 pixels

questions.explanation: Compute 168² − 140² = 28,224 − 19,600 = 8,624. The square root is about 92.9, and doubling it gives about 186 pixels. A row near the top of a round screen is much narrower than the full width. The value 336 would be the width at the center row, and 280 would simply double the distance from the center.

questions.question_text: What does `color565(0, 255, 255)`, which is cyan, return?

options.A: `0xFFFF`
options.D: `0xFFE0`

questions.explanation: Red is 0, so the top five bits are zero. Green at 255 keeps its top six bits, which gives `0x07E0`, and blue at 255 keeps its top five bits, which gives `0x001F`. Combining them gives `0x07FF`. The value `0xF81F` is red plus blue, which is magenta, and `0xFFE0` is red plus green, which is yellow.

questions.question_text: A digital face shows an 8-character time with 16-pixel-wide characters, and `CENTER_X` is 180. What `x` position centers the text?
questions.explanation: The text width is 8 × 16 = 128 pixels. Half of that is 64, so the starting position is 180 − 64 = 116. This matches the chapter's formula `x = CENTER_X - (len(msg) * 16) // 2`. Formatting the time to a constant width with zero padding means each new value covers the old one exactly, so the screen never needs clearing.

questions.question_text: On a direct write display, erasing the old second hand also cuts a gap in a numeral it crossed. What is the best design response?

options.A: Lay out the dial so hands never reach the ticks and numerals, avoiding repairs
options.B: Redraw the entire screen every second so any damage is hidden
options.C: Call `show()` after each erase so the gap is filled in
options.D: Lower the SPI baudrate so the erase happens more slowly

questions.explanation: Every overlap between a moving hand and a static item costs an extra repair step. The kit's dial is designed so the ticks sit outside the longest hand and the numerals lie outside the minute and hour hands, so few things can be damaged by an erase. Redrawing everything each second flickers on a direct write display, and the GC9B72 has no `show()` call.

questions.question_text: On a new color display, reds appear blue and blues appear red. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: RGB565 is not able to store the color red
options.B: The display expects BGR channel order, or the two bytes of each color are swapped
options.C: The backlight pin is wired to 3.3 V instead of a GPIO pin
options.D: The viewing angle of the panel is set too wide

questions.explanation: When red and blue trade places, the display expects the channels in a different order (BGR instead of RGB), or the two bytes of each 16-bit color are swapped. Most drivers have a setting for this, so check the driver's options before rewriting any of your colors. The backlight wiring affects brightness only, and viewing angle changes how colors look from the side.

questions.question_text: What supply voltage does a WS2812B NeoPixel strip use?

options.B: 5 V

questions.explanation: The WS2812B runs from 5 V power, receives data on a single wire at 800 kHz, and takes 24 bits per pixel, which is 8 each for green, red, and blue. The strip wants a data signal near its supply voltage, while the Pico gives 3.3 V. For short wires this usually works, and a level shifter helps if the first pixels flicker.

questions.question_text: Which call sends the pixel colors you set to a NeoPixel strip?

options.A: `np.show()`
options.B: `np.fill()`
options.C: `np.update()`
options.D: `np.write()`

questions.explanation: Setting `np[0] = (255, 0, 0)` changes only the colors stored in memory. Nothing lights up until `np.write()` sends the data down the strip, so you can update every pixel and then show them all at the same instant. The `fill()` method sets all pixels to one color in memory. The `show()` name belongs to OLED framebuffer displays, not to NeoPixels.

questions.question_text: Why must the NeoPixel strip's ground be connected to the Pico's ground?

options.A: It lets the strip draw its power from the Pico's 3.3 V pin
options.B: It makes the strip brighter than it would be otherwise
options.C: The data signal is measured relative to ground, so the strip ignores it without a shared ground
options.D: It lets the Pico read the colors that the strip is currently showing

questions.explanation: A voltage is always measured between two points, so the strip needs the same ground reference as the Pico to interpret the data signal. Without a shared ground the strip lights randomly or not at all. Connect ground first, add a 300 to 500 ohm resistor on the data line, and then apply power. A large capacitor across the strip's supply absorbs the surge when the LEDs switch on.

questions.question_text: What is the job of the latch pin on a 74HC595?

options.A: It copies the shifted bits to the outputs all at once, so outputs do not flicker while data moves in
options.B: It sets the speed at which data is shifted into the chip
options.C: It selects whether the chip receives data most significant bit first or least significant bit first
options.D: It turns the eight outputs off to save power between updates

questions.explanation: The 74HC595 has a shift register that collects bits and a separate storage register that drives the outputs. Pulsing the latch pin copies the shift register into the storage register in one instant, so all eight outputs change at exactly the same moment. Without the latch, the outputs would flicker as bits slid along. The clock pin, not the latch, controls the shifting.

questions.question_text: Why is the HSV color model a good choice for making a rainbow on a NeoPixel ring?

options.A: HSV uses fewer bits than RGB, so the strip draws less current
options.B: MicroPython can send HSV values to the strip without any conversion
options.C: HSV colors are always brighter than the same colors in RGB
options.D: Hue is an angle on a color wheel, so changing only hue moves through the rainbow

questions.explanation: HSV describes a color with hue, saturation, and value. Changing only the hue moves around the color wheel, and changing only the value changes the brightness. Giving pixel `i` of `N` the hue 360 × i / N paints a rainbow, and a growing offset rotates it. The strip itself still needs RGB, so the program converts with `hsv_to_rgb()`.

questions.question_text: About how much current can 30 NeoPixels draw if all are white at 50 percent brightness, using 60 mA per pixel at full brightness?

options.A: About 90 mA
options.B: About 900 mA
options.C: About 1.8 A
options.D: About 450 mA

questions.explanation: Use I = N × 60 mA × brightness fraction, which gives 30 × 60 × 0.5 = 900 mA. That is more than a USB port can supply, so this design would need a separate 5 V supply with its ground tied to the Pico's ground. Option C is the current at full brightness, and the plan should always cover the maximum your program can light up.

questions.question_text: An 8 × 8 NeoPixel matrix is wired in a zigzag, where odd rows run backward. Using `index = y * width + (x if y % 2 == 0 else width - 1 - x)`, what is the strip index of the pixel at x = 2, y = 3?
questions.explanation: Row 3 is odd, so the row runs backward and x becomes 8 − 1 − 2 = 5. The index is 3 × 8 + 5 = 29. Option A, 26, forgets the reversal and uses x directly. Converting (x, y) coordinates to a strip index lets you draw on the matrix with the same coordinate ideas used for displays in Chapter 12.

questions.question_text: On a binary clock row for minutes, which place-value pixels are lit to show the minute value 45?

options.A: The 32, 8, 4, and 1 pixels
options.B: The 32, 16, 8, and 4 pixels
options.C: The 32, 8, 2, and 1 pixels
options.D: The 16, 8, 4, and 1 pixels

questions.explanation: Break 45 into place values: 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 45. Minutes need 6 bits because the maximum of 59 is 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 + 1. A lit pixel is a 1 and an unlit pixel is a 0, so bits 5, 3, 2, and 0 are on. Option B sums to 60, option C to 43, and option D to 29.

questions.question_text: Four 74HC595 chips are chained to drive a four-digit seven-segment clock with 32 outputs. How many Pico pins are needed, and why?

options.A: 32 pins, because each output needs its own wire from the Pico
options.B: 12 pins, because each chip needs data, clock, and latch wires
options.C: 8 pins, because each byte needs eight data wires
options.D: 3 pins, because the chips share clock and latch lines and pass data along through QH'

questions.explanation: The QH' output passes the bit that falls off the end to the next chip's SER input, and the chips share the clock and latch lines. Together they act as one long register, so you send four bytes and update all 32 outputs using only data, clock, and latch pins. This design needs no multiplexing because every segment stays lit on its own.

questions.question_text: A 30-pixel strip lights all pixels at full white from the Pico's USB 5 V pin, and the Pico keeps resetting. What is the best fix?

options.A: Add a 10 kΩ resistor in series with the data line
options.B: Lower the brightness and power the strip from a separate 5 V supply with a shared ground
options.C: Power the strip from the 3.3 V pin so it draws less current
options.D: Raise the data rate so the pixels update faster

questions.explanation: Thirty pixels at full white can draw 30 × 60 mA = 1.8 A, far more than the roughly 500 mA that USB provides, so the supply sags and the Pico resets. Lower the brightness, since values of 10 to 60 are plenty for an indoor clock, and power the strip from a separate 5 V supply whose ground is tied to the Pico's ground. A larger data resistor or a faster data rate does not reduce current.

questions.question_text: What setting determines the pitch of a tone made with PWM?

options.A: The duty cycle of the signal
options.B: The supply voltage of the Pico
options.C: The GPIO pin number that is used
options.D: The frequency of the signal

questions.explanation: Pitch depends on frequency, the number of vibrations per second, so `buzzer.freq(440)` plays the note A above middle C. The duty cycle sets the tone's character and, to a small extent, its loudness. A higher note is nothing more than a faster wiggle, and doubling the frequency raises the pitch by one octave.

questions.question_text: Which type of piezo buzzer needs a PWM signal and lets you play melodies?

options.A: A passive buzzer
options.B: An active buzzer
options.C: Both types, equally
options.D: Neither type

questions.explanation: A passive buzzer has no oscillator of its own, so it needs a PWM signal and you choose the pitch. An active buzzer has a built-in oscillator and beeps at one fixed pitch when powered. A quick test tells them apart: an active buzzer connected to 3.3 V beeps by itself, but a passive one only clicks.

questions.question_text: Why should an 8 ohm speaker not be connected directly to a GPIO pin?

options.A: Speakers only work with 5 V signals and cannot use 3.3 V
options.B: A pin cannot produce frequencies in the range that speakers need
options.C: The speaker would ask for about 410 mA, far more than a pin can safely supply
options.D: Speakers need an I2S connection and cannot work with PWM

questions.explanation: By Ohm's Law, 3.3 V across 8 Ω asks for roughly 410 mA, many times what a GPIO pin can give, and it can damage the pin. Use a small amplifier module or a transistor between the pin and the speaker. A piezo buzzer draws only a few milliamps and can be wired straight to a pin.

questions.question_text: At a sampling rate of 16,000 samples per second, what is the highest pitch that can be reproduced?
questions.explanation: The Nyquist limit says the highest reproducible frequency is half the sampling rate, so 16,000 / 2 = 8,000 Hz. That is plenty for beeps and speech. CDs use 44,100 samples per second so they can reach 22,050 Hz, above human hearing. Higher rates cost more memory and bus time because each sample must be delivered on time.

questions.question_text: Why does an alarm program use a `fired` flag?

options.A: It speeds up the comparison between the current time and the alarm time
options.B: It stores the snooze time so the alarm can ring again later
options.C: It lets the alarm ring even when the seconds are not exactly 0
options.D: It makes the alarm ring once during the matching minute instead of restarting after being stopped

questions.explanation: The alarm condition `h == alarm_h and m == alarm_m` stays true for a whole minute. Without a flag, the alarm would start ringing again right after you stopped it, until the minute passed. The `fired` flag is set when the alarm starts and cleared once the minute is over. Comparing only the hour and minute is what lets the alarm still fire if the loop was busy at second 0.

questions.question_text: Using f = 440 × 2^(n/12), what is the frequency of the note 12 semitones below A440?

options.A: 220 Hz
options.B: 110 Hz
options.C: 330 Hz

questions.explanation: With n = −12 the formula gives 440 × 2^(−1) = 220 Hz. Going up or down by an octave, which is 12 semitones, exactly doubles or halves the frequency. The value 261.6 Hz is middle C, which is 9 semitones below A440, and 110 Hz would be two octaves down.

questions.question_text: What does `snooze(22, 58, 9)` return if it adds minutes using seconds since midnight and wraps at 86,400?
questions.explanation: The alarm at 22:58 is 82,680 seconds after midnight, and adding 9 minutes (540 seconds) gives 83,220. Dividing by 3,600 gives hour 23 with 420 seconds left over, which is 7 minutes. Working in seconds handles the carry automatically, and the `% 86400` wraps correctly past midnight. A minute value of 67 is impossible on a clock.

questions.question_text: How many bytes per second does 22,050 Hz, 16-bit, stereo (2 channels) audio need?

options.A: 22,050 bytes per second
options.B: 44,100 bytes per second
options.C: 88,200 bytes per second
options.D: 352,800 bytes per second

questions.explanation: Use data rate = rate × (bits / 8) × channels. Here that is 22,050 × 2 × 2 = 88,200 bytes per second. Mono audio would need half as much, 44,100 bytes per second. These numbers show why a long recording will not fit in the Pico's RAM and must be generated on the fly or streamed from flash.

questions.question_text: An alarm plays its tone list with `sleep_ms()` between notes, and pressing snooze does nothing until the whole tune ends. What is the cause and the fix?

options.A: The sleeps stop the loop from checking buttons; step through the tones with `ticks_diff()` instead
options.B: The buzzer is an active type; replace it with a passive one
options.C: The snooze button needs an external pull-up resistor to be read
options.D: The tones are too long; shorten each note to under 50 ms

questions.explanation: While the program sleeps, it does nothing else, so it cannot read buttons or update the display. A better design keeps an index into the tone list and a start time, and moves on when `ticks_diff()` says the current note is finished, checking the buttons on every pass of the loop. An alarm that freezes the whole clock while beeping is a bad alarm.

questions.question_text: A stopwatch resumes after a pause but the displayed total jumps back to near zero. What is the most likely bug?

options.A: The `ticks_ms()` counter wrapped around during the pause
options.B: The loop delay of 50 ms is too short to measure time
options.C: The button was configured without `Pin.PULL_UP`
options.D: The elapsed time was not saved into the accumulated total before the pause

questions.explanation: When the stopwatch stops, it must save the elapsed time so far into a `saved` value. On restart it takes a new start tick and adds the saved time to what has elapsed since. If the pause step skips the save, the total restarts from the new start tick. The `ticks_ms()` counter wraps only after about 12.4 days, and `ticks_diff()` handles that anyway.

questions.question_text: Which Pico pins can be used as analog (ADC) inputs?

options.A: GP0, GP1, and GP2
options.B: GP26, GP27, and GP28
options.C: GP14, GP15, and GP16
options.D: Any GPIO pin on the board

questions.explanation: The Pico's ADC has three usable inputs on GP26, GP27, and GP28, which are channels ADC0, ADC1, and ADC2. They measure voltages from 0 V to 3.3 V. The other pins can only tell 0 from 1. Because ADC readings jitter a little even when nothing changes, it helps to read the pin 8 or 16 times and use the average.

questions.question_text: The RP2040 ADC has 12 bits of resolution, yet `read_u16()` returns values from 0 to 65,535. Why?

options.A: The RP2040 hardware contains a separate 16-bit converter for each pin
options.B: The value is the voltage in millivolts, which can reach 65,535
options.C: The reading counts the number of times the pin was sampled each second
options.D: MicroPython scales the 12-bit result up to 16 bits so the range is always the same

questions.explanation: The hardware gives 2^12 = 4,096 levels, and MicroPython scales the result to a 16-bit range, so the value runs from 0 to 65,535 no matter how many bits the hardware has. To convert to volts, multiply by 3.3 and divide by 65,535. A reading of 32,768 is about half of full scale, or 1.65 V.

questions.question_text: How does hysteresis stop a display from flickering when the room light hovers near a threshold?

options.A: It uses two thresholds with a dead zone, so noise near the line does not toggle the output
options.B: It averages 16 readings so the sensor value never changes at all
options.C: It slows the PWM frequency of the backlight below 1 kHz
options.D: It rounds the light reading to the nearest whole brightness level

questions.explanation: With one threshold, noise near the line makes the output chatter. Hysteresis uses a higher threshold to switch up and a lower one to switch back down. The gap between them is a dead zone where nothing changes, so small noise falls inside it. This is the same idea as debouncing a button in Chapter 7, and thermostats use it so a furnace does not switch on and off every few seconds.

questions.question_text: An LDR is wired in a divider with a 10 kΩ fixed resistor between the ADC pin and ground, and 3.3 V on the LDR side. What is Vout when the LDR is 5 kΩ?
questions.explanation: The formula is Vout = 3.3 × R_fixed / (R_LDR + R_fixed), which gives 3.3 × 10 / (5 + 10) = 2.2 V. With this wiring a brighter room lowers the LDR's resistance and raises Vout, so a bigger ADC reading means brighter light. The value 0.55 V is the output for a dim room, where the LDR is about 50 kΩ.

questions.question_text: A clock draws an average of 50 mA from a 2,000 mAh battery. Using the 0.8 factor, about how long will it run?

options.A: About 40 hours
options.B: About 32 hours
options.C: About 25 hours
options.D: About 16 hours

questions.explanation: The runtime formula is capacity × 0.8 divided by average current, so 2,000 × 0.8 / 50 = 32 hours. The 0.8 factor allows for the fact that batteries never deliver their full labeled capacity. Leaving it out would give 40 hours, which is too optimistic. Measure your own current by placing a multimeter in series with the power wire.

questions.question_text: Which of these power sources should NOT be connected to the Pico's VSYS pin, whose limit is 5.5 V?

options.A: A 2 × AA pack at 3.0 V
options.B: A 3 × AA pack at 4.5 V
options.C: A single LiPo cell at 3.7 V
options.D: A 4 × AA alkaline pack at 6.0 V

questions.explanation: The VSYS pin accepts 1.8 V to 5.5 V, and the board's regulator converts that to 3.3 V. Four alkaline AA cells give 6.0 V, which exceeds the limit. A 3 × AA pack at 4.5 V is the recommended choice, and the 2 × AA pack and the LiPo cell are both inside the allowed range.

questions.question_text: A LiPo battery is wired to a watch board that has no protection circuit. Why is it risky to connect the connector with reversed polarity?

options.A: Reversed polarity can destroy the board or even start a fire
options.B: Reversed polarity only makes the battery charge more slowly
options.C: Reversed polarity makes the display show colors in the wrong order
options.D: Reversed polarity is harmless because LiPo cells are 3.7 V

questions.explanation: LiPo connectors are not always standardized, and reversing the polarity can destroy a board or start a fire. LiPo cells also need a charging circuit designed for lithium cells, ideally with a protection circuit against over-discharge and short circuits. Never discharge one below about 3.0 V, puncture or crush it, or charge one that is swollen.

questions.question_text: A battery-powered Pico runs fine until the WiFi sync starts, and then it resets. The battery is nearly empty. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The hysteresis thresholds are set too close together
options.B: The ADC reading has overflowed its 16-bit range
options.C: A brownout: the WiFi surge makes the weak battery sag below what the chip needs
options.D: The LDR divider has a fixed resistor that is too small

questions.explanation: A brownout is when the supply voltage sags below what the chip needs, but not all the way to zero. It often happens when a load surges, such as WiFi transmission, a backlight, or NeoPixels turning on, and the battery or a thin wire cannot deliver the current. Print `machine.reset_cause()` at startup to see if resets are power problems. Fixes include a fresher battery and a capacitor near the power pins.

questions.question_text: A student integrates a gyroscope's rotation rate to estimate an angle. After a minute with the board sitting still, the angle has slowly wandered. What explains this, and what is a good remedy?

options.A: The gyroscope measures gravity, so it cannot ever be still
options.B: Tiny errors add up as the rate is integrated, so combine it with the accelerometer's stable tilt
options.C: The I2C address conflicts with the DS3231, so the gyroscope returns random values
options.D: The ADC noise adds to the rate, so the reading should be averaged 16 times

questions.explanation: A gyroscope reports how fast the board is rotating, not which way is down. Adding up (integrating) the rate gives an angle, but tiny errors accumulate, so the angle drifts. An accelerometer gives a stable but noisy tilt from gravity. The two sensors complement each other: the gyroscope is smooth but drifts, and the accelerometer is stable but noisy.

questions.question_text: A smartwatch draws about 85 mA, and its backlight alone uses about 60 mA. Which change would save the most battery life?

options.A: Replace the DS3231 with a different RTC chip
options.B: Use shorter wires between the display and the Pico
options.C: Raise the CPU speed so that the program finishes sooner
options.D: Dim the backlight and sleep between updates

questions.explanation: The display is the biggest target for savings. In the chapter's example, dimming the backlight from 60 mA to 20 mA cuts the total from 85 mA to about 45 mA and roughly doubles the runtime. Sleeping between updates with a timer or RTC alarm as the wake source saves still more. The DS3231 uses under 1 mA, so replacing it would save almost nothing.

questions.question_text: Which signal on an e-paper module tells the Pico that the display is still refreshing?

options.A: D/C
options.B: /RST
options.C: BUSY
options.D: /CS

questions.explanation: Most e-paper modules connect over SPI with one extra signal, BUSY. Refreshing takes a while, and the display raises BUSY to say it is still updating. Your program should wait for BUSY to clear before sending more data. The D/C pin separates commands from data, /RST restarts the chip, and /CS selects the device on the SPI bus.

questions.question_text: What does it mean to say that an e-paper display is bistable?

options.A: It has two backlights, one for the day and one for the night
options.B: It has two stable states that it keeps without power, so power is needed only to change a pixel
options.C: It can show only two colors, black and white, at the same time
options.D: It uses two SPI buses to double the speed of each refresh

questions.explanation: A bistable display, like a light switch that stays where you flip it, holds either state with no power at all. E-paper particles stay where the electric field left them, so energy is used only to change a pixel, never to hold one. A clock that updates once a minute therefore spends nearly all its time drawing zero power, and a small battery can last for months.

questions.question_text: What is e-paper ghosting, and what clears it?

options.A: A burn-in that is permanent and requires replacing the panel
options.B: A flicker caused by a backlight that is dimmed with PWM
options.C: A color shift that appears when the panel is viewed from the side
options.D: A faint shadow of the previous image, which a full refresh clears

questions.explanation: Ghosting is a faint shadow of the previous image that remains after a refresh, because the particles do not move all the way each time. It is most noticeable in a large dark area that was replaced with white. It is not permanent: a full refresh clears it. The best defense is a schedule that mixes quick partial updates with an occasional full one.

questions.question_text: A DHT22 sensor reports 25 °C. What is that in degrees Fahrenheit, using F = C × 9/5 + 32?
questions.explanation: Multiply 25 by 9/5 to get 45, then add 32 to get 77 °F. The value 45 results from forgetting the final 32, and 57 comes from simply adding 32 to the Celsius number. For display, round the result with `round(f)`. The built-in 8 by 8 font has no degree symbol, so draw a small circle next to the number or use a custom font.

questions.question_text: A clock redraws its e-paper display once every minute, but only when the minute changes. How many refreshes happen in one day?
questions.explanation: There are 24 hours of 60 minutes each in a day, so 24 × 60 = 1,440 refreshes, which is well within a panel's rating of about a million updates. The test `if m != last_minute` is what turns a loop that runs every second into a refresh that happens once a minute. Refreshing 86,400 times a day, once per second, would wear the panel and waste energy.

questions.question_text: A weather display reads its indoor sensor every 5 minutes. How many indoor readings occur in one hour?
questions.explanation: An hour has 60 minutes, and 60 / 5 = 12 readings. Indoor temperature and humidity change slowly, so reading every 5 to 10 minutes is enough. The time display updates every minute, and the outdoor forecast every 1 to 3 hours. Matching each item's update schedule to how fast it changes saves power, especially for the forecast, since each fetch needs WiFi.

questions.question_text: An e-paper clock loses power and keeps showing 10:42 while the real time is 11:30. What design risk does this show?

options.A: The panel holds its image without power, so a stopped clock looks normal but is wrong
options.B: The panel loses its image immediately, so the display goes blank
options.C: The panel keeps updating itself from the internet without any power
options.D: The panel is showing ghosting, which will clear on its own after a few minutes

questions.explanation: Because e-paper is bistable, it still shows the last time it drew when power fails, looking perfectly normal but wrong. A clock that cannot show it has stopped is confusing. A robust design also shows when it last synced, or displays a small warning if the time source fails. Ghosting is a different effect, a faint remnant of an earlier image.

questions.question_text: After several days of partial refreshes only, an e-paper clock shows faint old digits smeared behind the current time. What is the cause and the fix?

options.A: The BUSY pin is not wired, so the fix is to add a pull-up resistor
options.B: The SPI baudrate is too high, so the fix is to lower it to 1 MHz
options.C: The panel is a three-color model, so the fix is to switch to black and white
options.D: Partial updates build up ghosting, so force a full refresh about every 30 partials and once a day

questions.explanation: Partial updates are fast and quiet, but each one leaves a little more ghosting. A good strategy is a partial refresh each minute, a full refresh after about 30 partial updates, and a full refresh at least once a day. Keeping a counter of partial refreshes takes only two lines of code. A wiring or baudrate problem would corrupt the whole image, not leave faint old digits.

questions.question_text: Which display is the best choice for a clock on a sunny porch that must run for weeks on a small battery and updates once a minute?

options.A: A TM1637 LED module
options.B: A round GC9A01 color TFT
options.C: An e-paper display
options.D: A NeoPixel ring

questions.explanation: E-paper reflects room light, so it is readable in bright sun, and it uses power only when the picture changes, so a once-a-minute clock can last weeks or months on a small battery. LEDs and NeoPixels are hard to read in direct sunlight and draw power all the time they are lit. A color TFT's backlight is the largest power consumer on the display.

questions.question_text: Which design is the most appropriate plan for a battery-powered weather station display?

options.A: Update time every minute, indoor readings every 5 to 10 minutes, and the forecast every 1 to 3 hours with WiFi on only during the fetch and the last good value kept on failure
options.B: Fetch the forecast every second so that the display is always up to date
options.C: Keep WiFi on all the time and stop the program if a fetch ever fails
options.D: Redraw every item with a full refresh each second to avoid ghosting

questions.explanation: Each piece of data should have its own update schedule matched to how fast it changes. WiFi should be on only for the brief moment of a fetch, and the program should plan for failure by keeping the last good value or showing dashes such as `--`. Fetching every second wastes power and burdens the service, and refreshing a whole panel every second would wear it out quickly.

questions.question_text: In a must-should-could requirements list, what should be finished before you start any "could" item?

options.A: The enclosure for the clock
options.B: The final presentation slides
options.C: A second prototype of the whole clock
options.D: Every "must" item

questions.explanation: The must-should-could list protects you from over-promising. You finish every "must", such as showing the correct time, before touching a "could", such as an alarm. Planning in this order, with steps that each end in something you can see working, means you always have a working version to fall back on if time runs short.

questions.question_text: Why does the chapter recommend testing each hardware part by itself before combining them?

options.A: A part that misbehaves alone will misbehave in the finished clock, and its fault is easier to find when it is the only thing connected
options.B: Parts that are tested alone no longer need to be tested again once they are combined
options.C: Individual tests are required by the Pico before it will run a program
options.D: Testing a part alone makes it more accurate when it is later connected

questions.explanation: Hardware testing checks each physical part by itself, from the bottom up: power, wires, the Pico, buttons, I2C devices, and then the display. When you add a new part, add only that part and then test, so a failure points to exactly one change. Integration testing is still needed afterward, because two parts that work alone can fail as a pair.

questions.question_text: Why does a display often flash or blink if the program clears the whole screen before every update?

options.A: Clearing the screen resets the SPI baudrate to a lower value
options.B: Clearing the screen erases the display driver from memory
options.C: For a moment the viewer sees a blank screen before the new picture is drawn
options.D: Clearing the screen turns off the backlight until the next restart

questions.explanation: On direct write screens, a clear followed by a redraw shows a blank screen in between, which looks like a flash. The fixes, in order of effectiveness, are to avoid clearing by drawing text with a background color, to draw the static parts once, to erase only the old bounding box, and to update less often. Also check the supply, because a backlight or WiFi that dips the voltage can cause visible flicker.

questions.question_text: A decision matrix gives readability a weight of 3, cost a weight of 4, and power a weight of 2. Design X scores 4, 3, and 5 on those qualities, and Design Y scores 5, 2, and 3. Which design wins?

options.A: Design Y, with a weighted total of 29
options.B: Design X, with a weighted total of 34
options.C: Design X, with a weighted total of 12
options.D: Neither, because the totals tie at 31

questions.explanation: Multiply each score by its weight and add. For Design X: 3 × 4 + 4 × 3 + 2 × 5 = 12 + 12 + 10 = 34. For Design Y: 3 × 5 + 4 × 2 + 2 × 3 = 15 + 8 + 6 = 29. Design X wins because it does better on the heavily weighted cost. Different weights could reverse the result, which is why the weights capture your own priorities.

questions.question_text: A bill of materials totals \$17.89. Adding a 15 percent allowance for spares, about what budget should you plan?

options.A: About $20.57
options.B: About $18.04
options.C: About $32.89
options.D: About $17.89

questions.explanation: Fifteen percent of \$17.89 is about \$2.68, so the planned budget is \$17.89 + \$2.68 = \$20.57. A good BOM includes 10 to 20 percent extra for spares because jumper wires and cheap modules do fail. Adding just 15 cents gives option B, and adding 15 dollars gives option C. Both misread what a percentage allowance means.

questions.question_text: An AI-written alarm program uses `sleep(60)` in its main loop, and pressing the buttons seems to do nothing for up to a minute. What is the diagnosis?

options.A: The buttons need pull-down resistors instead of pull-ups
options.B: The AI used physical pin numbers instead of GP numbers
options.C: The `sleep()` function is not available in MicroPython
options.D: The blocking sleep stops the loop from checking buttons; non-blocking `ticks_ms()` timing is needed

questions.explanation: While the program sleeps it does nothing else, so presses during the sleep are never noticed. Blocking code is one of the common problems in AI-generated programs, along with regular-Python-only calls, wrong pin numbering, invented driver calls, and missing setup. The fix is the non-blocking `ticks_diff()` pattern from earlier chapters. Run every line on the real board and verify the result.

questions.question_text: A logic analyzer capture shows the address byte on an I2C bus, but the ninth clock pulse shows no acknowledgment. What does this tell you?

options.A: The device answered correctly but the baudrate is too low
options.B: The device did not respond, so check the address, the wiring, and the pull-ups
options.C: The Pico's clock is running too fast for the device
options.D: The device acknowledged but then sent no data bytes

questions.explanation: After the address byte, an I2C device that heard its address pulls SDA low during the ninth clock pulse to acknowledge. No acknowledgment means the device did not respond: the address is wrong, the wiring is wrong, or the pull-up resistors are missing. A logic analyzer is the electronics version of a print statement, because it shows what is actually happening on the wires.

questions.question_text: A clock shows the wrong date right after midnight on December 31. What is the best first step in a systematic debugging plan?

options.A: Rewrite all of the date code from scratch
options.B: Replace the DS3231 with a new module
options.C: Reproduce it quickly by setting the time to 23:59:50 on December 31 and watching the rollover
options.D: Paste the code into an AI tool and use whatever it returns without testing

questions.explanation: Systematic debugging starts by reproducing the bug on purpose, every time. Setting the clock to 23:59:50 and watching ten seconds is far faster than waiting for a year to end. After that, you form one hypothesis, run one test, and change one thing at a time. Rewriting code or replacing parts without a hypothesis is random poking and teaches you nothing.

questions.question_text: A student says, "The AI wrote this code, so if it fails, it is not my responsibility." Which response is best?

options.A: You are responsible for every line you submit, so run it on the real board and be able to explain it
options.B: That is correct, because AI-written code is always tested before it is given out
options.C: That is correct as long as you mention which AI tool wrote the code
options.D: That is correct if the program compiles without any errors

questions.explanation: AI tools produce a draft from a fast but overconfident assistant. They invent functions that do not exist in MicroPython and say so with total confidence. You are responsible for every line you submit, no matter who or what wrote it. If you cannot explain the code, you are not finished: ask the AI to explain it, then check the explanation against the documentation.

questions.question_text: Which plan is the best way to organize a five-to-seven-minute final presentation of a clock project?

options.A: Read the program aloud line by line for the full time
options.B: Goal, live demo with a backup video, trade-offs, one bug found by systematic debugging, BOM total, AI use, and next steps
options.C: Show only the finished clock and leave out anything that went wrong
options.D: Show only the live demo and skip the parts list and the testing story

questions.explanation: A strong presentation covers the goal, a live demo with a backup video in case something fails, the design trade-offs, one bug and how you found it, the bill of materials and its total, how you used AI and one thing it got wrong, and your next steps. Presenters are judged on the whole process, not only the finished object, so a clock debugged with clear thinking can beat one that worked by luck.
